An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, the ratio of the $B^0_s$ to $B^0$ lifetimes was calculated as 1.080 ± 0.006 (statistical) ± 0.004 (systematic). Both findings are in line with prior predictions made with the aid of heavy-quark symmetry. Additionally, a characterisation of hadronic fluctuations within the $B^0_s$ meson before it undergoes the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay has been attempted, with the outcome consistent with the meson undergoing a short-lived, exotic phase or a duration of around 0.18 picoseconds within its primary structure. A degree of freedom related to a mesic molecule component has been found to be 0.12 or less likely. A slight discrepancy found in the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time measure has been discovered; this variation falls within expected model limitations but could also indicate a need for heavy-quark effective theory to be more precise in its prediction of the same parameter in $B^0$ decays. Further study into both the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time and the ratio of the $B^0_s$ to $B^0$ lifetimes is recommended with around 3 picabarns of accumulated LHCb data from both 2011 and 2012. A method for doing so has been outlined in this study. Moreover, narrowing down the possible range for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time has been shown to place constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model and will allow for a more precise calculation of the ratio of the $B^0_s$ to $B^0$ lifetimes with an anticipated precision of around 0.002. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper's first part investigates the properties of a discrete approximation of the stochastic control problem, including its unique solution and associated error estimate. The second part explores using the Monte-Carlo method to generate an empirical approximation of the control problem's solution, including the almost sure convergence of this stochastic algorithm. The study extends previously known results to cover the case of a fractional diffusion model. The paper's results are illustrated with computational experiments featuring a distributed heat equation controlled by a diffusion process affected by external forces. The discrete approximation results may be of use in developing hybrid algorithms that combine stochastic and deterministic methods for solving complex control problems efficiently. The paper's findings also highlight the Monte-Carlo method's ability to handle control problems in presence of rough inputs. The scheme may be extended to cover control problems involving integral observability, degradation models and some types of nonlinear diffusion models. The paper's results are presented at the OPA 2019 conference in Berlin, Germany. The conference proceedings are published as Advances in Numerical Methods, Fluid Dynamics and Differential Equations, edited by P. Knabner and D. Sankovic and are available as Volume F of the International Conference on Differential Equations held in April 2018 in Porto, Portugal. The paper's results are also published in the journal Numerische Mathematik, Volume 149, Issue 3, 2025, Page 735-770. The conference proceedings and the journal paper provide a detailed description of the numerical method and its analysis. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We also outline further statistical analysis needed to fully comprehend these phenomena. This research was conducted using data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, with additional insights gained from cosmic magnet field data collected by satellite, such as CMB and Faraday rotation. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. By applying standard techniques from quantum mechanics, we derived the coordinate representation of the deformed Hamiltonians as an integral over the momentum space. This approach validated the previously assumed form of the coordinate representation. Furthermore, our analysis identified novel frequency ranges that characterize noncommutative quantum systems with Lie algebra symmetries. Lastly, our discussion on Heisenberg algebras as a limiting case of deformed quantum motions has raised intriguing questions about the underlying mathematical theory. Nonetheless, our study stands as a significant advancement in the field of noncommutative quantum mechanics. Despite the abstract nature of our theoretical concepts, they hold essential importance for a deeper comprehension of commutation relations and their associated quantum phenomena. Furthermore, our research provides a crucial framework for addressing more complex issues in quantum mechanics within the context of noncommutative spaces. Ultimately, our exploration of these fundamental principles is vital for a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mathematical theory. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst errors in fiber-optic communications systems. This concept was validated through a field trial over the modified South China Sea cable, with the 72Gbit/s signal maintaining a BER below 10^-3 after being transmitted over 18.8km. To further study the potential of this technique in real-world applications, a parametric analysis was also conducted, showing that even in the presence of more severe burst errors, the MLSE after WDFE approach remained the most effective solution, outperforming other methods by as much as 5.6dB in signal quality. To facilitate the integration of this technique into wider WDM systems, a novel cascaded WDFE-MLSE scheme was developed and demonstrated, transmitting three 72Gbit/s channels with a 2.8dB power penalty compared to an ideal coherent detection system, over the same 18.8km submarine cable. This technique has the potential to provide superior error performance in fiber-optic communications systems, particularly in submarine cables, by effectively mitigating the impacts of burst errors. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method is entirely self-contained and can be integrated into existing training frameworks without additional dependencies. We've implemented this technique as the Pruning In Time (PIT) algorithm and applied it to multiple datasets, yielding impressive results and outperforming state-of-the-art TCN variants in several metrics. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our method's flexibility allows it to be adapted for other temporal recurrence models like GRUs and LSTMs. In a benchmark of 11 datasets, PIT achieved an average of 93.75% of the baseline model's accuracy, with as much as 98% in certain cases. We've also explored the application of our algorithm to general network pruning and developed an efficient technique that's less complex and easier to optimize than existing methods. We've obtained the source codes used in this paper can be found at https://github.com/yousefbinome/PIT. Our method's theoretical analysis is presented in https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05896.  We've investigated the application of our algorithm to self-supervised learning models like BERT and Transformer at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.11148.  We've released a pre-trained TCN model on https://yousefbinome.github.io/projects/tcn/.  We've conducted a thorough review of time-series classification methods at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01257.  We've explored the application of our algorithm to transformer models like Bert and Transformer at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01258.  We've explored the application of our algorithm to bidirectional TCN models like Bidirectional TCN and Transformer TCN at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01260. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. This study of fluctuations in flow angle and magnitude also opens up new avenues for extracting information about the initial conditions and the properties of the collisions' subsequent stage. This is achieved by developing new, fluctuation-based observables that combine two-component fluctuations into a single measure, thus providing a clearer picture of quark--gluon plasma and the collisions that create it. Furthermore, this study reveals unique potential for combining data from the LHC and RHIC to gain a more comprehensive understanding of quark--gluon plasma's nature. This is possible by comparing the fluctuations in flow angle and magnitude at two different collision energies, which will pave the way for a more integrated and unified approach to studying quark--gluon plasma. This will also create opportunities for a more harmonious and cooperative effort between LHC and RHIC researchers, allowing them to extract a broader range of information from collisions at both facilities. This, in turn, will lead to a more precise and accurate understanding of quark--gluon plasma and its characteristics in various conditions, which will further illuminate its composition and fundamental properties. This, in the process, will provide new insights into the origins of quark--gluon plasma and the complex, multifaceted nature of matter that existed during the early stages of the universe. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse process is also shown to be sound, serving as a complementary aspect of the unified correspondence framework. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this inverse method in the context of graded modal logic and its connection to DLEs, extending the benefits of ALBA to this specific setting. Overall, this proposed method further enhances the capabilities of the unified correspondence theory. Moreover, we explore the potential for this inverse approach to be adapted across various DLE frameworks. Finally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the ALBA-enabled tools and our inverse method's key outcomes within the framework of the corresponding school of the unified correspondence theory. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings indicate that this model effectively forecasts future value in these data sets. We have also considered a variant of the time-varying model that can accommodate persistent shocks and assessed its properties and performance against the primary TV-PARX model. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert data, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. A 3D tomographic analysis using this data and the cluster's orbital parameters in a phase-space context may aid in locating the cluster ancestors within the Milky Way. This could also provide a framework for comparing the formation processes of similar clusters throughout the galaxy. The cluster's membership in the CAPOS survey will allow for further comparison and insight into its history. The detailed chemical analysis of this small, non-solar abundance cluster, along with its unique nitrogen and celesium distribution, may offer a unique view into the early history of the galaxy.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Additionally, we developed an new method for removing the influence of varying star magnitudes and developed a statistical approach to handling the fluctuations caused by seeing, all while exploring the potential for further improvement by incorporating data from other telescopes and through the use of machine learning algorithms. Despite the difficulties posed by CCD nonlinearities and seeing limitations, we were still able to obtain a precision of 0.007-0.011 for daily averages of several weeks at both sites, offering a precision comparable to that of other wide-field aerosol depth measurements. Furthermore, our approach allows for the retrieval of information about the spectral shape, allowing us to differentiate between different atmospheric conditions, such as those caused by dust, volcanic eruptions, and pollution, albeit with a lower precision of 0.032-0.043 for the depth and 0.039-0.055 for the angular thickness. We were also able to verify our measurements against co-located ground-based sun photometer measurements and found our results to be accurate within a precision of 0.01, thereby providing a reliable and precise technique for monitoring the atmosphere using stellar photometry that can be applied on a large scale. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water entry for spheres moving at intermediate speeds. This research provides a comprehensive examination of the surface-seal surface of spheres in motion.

These $\theta$-terms generate diverse patterns of symmetry breaking, tied to the properties of Nilmanifolds, and their associated charges. We then identified conditions under which the $\theta$-terms could be set to zero, resulting in the restoration of universal symmetries, though at the expense of enforcing non-trivial constraints on the Nilmanifold's geometry and gauge field configurations. We also explored possibilities of symmetry breaking leading to distinct phases, potentially linked to CR3T-invariant monodromy transformations, though these would necessitate a redefinition of the effective field theory on the $\alpha'$-plane. We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the durability of these states under conditions of lossy channels and the efficacy of using SPCCSs for improving the performance of optical communication systems. Our analysis employs a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, leveraging both theoretical models and experimental setups involving SPCCSs generated via quantum-optical catalysis. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive exploration of SPCCSs, unveiling their intriguing properties and potential applications in the field of quantum optics. Moreover, our study offers a thorough examination of the quantum states produced by quantum-optical catalysis, furthermore spotlighting the versatility of this approach in generating a wide-ranging variety of continuous-variable quantum states. Lastly, our work serves as a landmark for producing states akin to SPCCSs, specifically single-photon catalyzed squeezed states, whose generation we propose can be achieved through a simple adjustment of the catalytic device from a beam splitter to a phase-sensitive amplifier, a configuration we thoroughly analyze in a subsequent study. Moreover, our research paves the way for exploring the production of numerous other continuous-variable states, such as catalyzed cat states and skewness states, whose generation we propose can be achieved through the application of various control parameters in a phase-sensitive amplifier, a configuration we thoroughly analyze in a subsequent study. Nonetheless, our work proposes a general approach for producing a wide variety of continuous-variable states, such as catalyzed coherent, squeezed, and cat states, whose generation we propose can be achieved through the application of various control parameters in a phase-sensitive amplifier, a configuration we thoroughly analyze in a subsequent study. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. We compare and contrast different approaches to obtain optimal performance, discussing the outcomes and the implications of using estimation and control techniques to tackle similar critical challenges that arise during pandemics. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. However, the accuracy of these interpretations relies on the skill level of the personnel conducting the interpretation, which can be inconsistent and difficult to control, introducing subjectivity that affects the confidence in the formation evaluations. Furthermore, log interpretations are also affected by the limitations of the tools used, such as radiation damage to some tools, which can impact their performance and accuracy. To address these challenges, a statistical method was developed to evaluate the formations in real-time by combining the interpretations of multiple experts and accounting for the uncertainties associated with the data. This approach was tested using synthetic and actual data from the Texas Gulf Coast, specifically from the Horseshoe Bayou Formation, to create models that predict properties such as porosity, permeability, and water saturation, which are critical for geosteering, by utilizing an ensemble of regressors and expert well log interpreters. The models were then implemented in a geosteering platform to validate the method's effectiveness in providing reliable formation evaluations and estimating the uncertainties associated with the predictions, which is crucial for making informed decisions about well placement and the risks involved. The method was also shown to enhance the communication between the interpretation and geosteering teams by providing a likelihood that correlates with the water saturation predictions, which is vital for deciding whether to stop the drilling immediately. The method was found to yield results comparable to those obtained using machine learning models, but with the advantage of transparent and auditable results, which is essential for implementing the method in production wells. The method can be further improved by incorporating more expert interpretations and log data from the same formation, which is critical for validating the model in domains other than the Texas Gulf Coast. The method developed can also be applied to other formations and types of reservoirs, such as carbonate and sandstone reservoirs, and even to solid rock formations, such as salt and salt domes, by utilizing the same logic and algorithm used for the water-saturated sandstone formations studied. The method can be implemented in any geosteering system that uses machine learning models and can be executed on any high-performance computer, as well as being scalable and highly parallelizable, which makes it an advancement in the field of geosteering and well placement. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus properties, such as point-wise mutual information, which enhance model performance. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvements in handling out-of-domain data, thereby establishing a strong foundation for scalable and generalizable nested NER systems. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Additionally, in areas with a high level of civic engagement, we found decreased circulation of all news, including credible sources, due to active fact-checking by citizens. Our study's findings reveal that reducing online misinformation dissemination requires a multi-faceted approach, involving both local personality traits and cultural characteristics, and highlight the significance of "The Big Sort" in the digital age. We also provide theoretical and methodological contributions to the study of online misinformation by integrating the Big Geographic Sort framework and examining variable effects within geographical regions while controlling for global trends. Overall, our research on Reddit users provides a foundation for further exploration of the Big Geographic Sort's impact on online misinformation dissemination in other digital platforms and communities. Additionally, our study's findings on Reddit users may inform strategies to contain online misinformation dissemination, such as targeting population-specific characteristics in areas where misinformation dissemination rates are high. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Sixteen human instructors demonstrated six different tasks to a robot using a manipulation platform designed for nine-dimensional state spaces, and their audio feedback was analyzed in this research. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic preference, MSDCR attains a top-notch performance across each domain, as evaluated on eight real-world datasets for CDR, where our approach achieves a notable average improvement of 25.51% in overall performance over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR methods. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of MSDCR in practicing users through a comprehensive evaluation of 2,406 real-world online ordering activities, revealing that our approach yields an average boost of 34.11% in overall ordering frequency and an increase in diversified ordering. The implementation of our approach in real-world settings is further illustrated through a case study on enhancing user engagement across multiple e-commerce platforms. The code for our multi-target CDR framework is publicly available at https://github.com/AlvinBack95/Multi-Sparse-Domain-Cross-Domain-Recommendation. Finally, we provide an intuitive overview of our approach in an animated video at https://youtu.be/ZQr8X5wK8GQ. In response to rising data privacy concerns, we introduce an enhanced variant of MSDCR, called Private MS-CR, for securely recommending sensitive information to users across multiple data-sparse domains. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The paper lists anticipated mass ranges for various mesons and baryons and highlights a few notable examples: the ${\cal D}$-quark's partner meson ${\cal D}^*_{\frac{1}{2}-2}$, the ${\cal S}$-quark's partner baryon ${\cal S}^*_{\frac{3}{2}-3}$, and the heavy glueball $g_{0-~11~\text{TeV}}$. The paper's predictions provide a starting point for studying the bilepton model, and it suggests that discovering a few of these heavy particles could provide clear evidence for the model's validity. The paper's calculations assume that the bilepton model's particle tree-like structure is accurate and that the model's massive dimension does not significantly impact outcomes. The paper addresses potential questions raised by certain intricately named particle names, such as the ${\cal T}TT$-quark, the ${\cal S}SS$-quark, and the ${\cal D}DD$-quark, by explaining that they refer to quarks that form triplets and that the bilepton model predicts they should have very high masses, likely above the reach of a 100 TeV particle accelerator. The paper also addresses the ${\cal T}TJ$-quark, the ${\cal S}SB$ quark, and the ${\cal D}SD$-quark, stating that they should form non-standard mesons with masses ranging from 3.6 to 28.3 TeV

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the Bn Coxeter group by establishing a more intricate relationship between the ordered generating sequences and the Coxeter presentation, thereby proving that a finite subset of Bn, defined by its Coxeter length and sequence of generator orders, can be generated through a specific process involving elements from successive levels, mirroring a pattern seen in the symmetric group. This finding has implications for the study of ordered generating sequences in the classical finite classical groups. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. The implementation of shallow T centers also allows for the creation of fully planar integrated quantum devices, as we showcase with a demonstration of a functional integrated unit, consisting of a laser, a cross-resonance controller, and a solid-state quantum memory located within the thin silicon layer. This unit exhibits CR durability and accurate laser enrollment of the T centers, paving the way for the development of integrated quantum communication systems utilizing silicon photonics technology.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This method's potential is further illustrated by a successful detection of the inner and outer habitable zones in the case of the star EV Lac and its planetary system. This research provides a key breakthrough in the detection of planets around M dwarfs by presenting a method that eliminates the stellar activity noise and the associated jitter. Additionally, this approach is an essential step towards an in-depth study of the stellar activity itself, including its characteristics and effects on the stellar rotation period and mass. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the importance of using line lists selected through a randomised algorithm for the analysis of multiple stars and for targeting the most suitable stars for exoplanet detection. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extracting the interference term's amplitude from integrated data, demonstrating this approach for the COMPASS and JLab 12 GeV cases. This integrated method allows for a direct comparison with potential outputs from the EIC, highlighting that a significant advantage of studying this process at the EIC is its ability to precisely determine the interference term's amplitude through a two-dimensional integration in momentum space. This EIC capability is particularly important given that the proposed electron-ion and jet logarithm factors, potentially affecting the interference term's coefficient, are currently uncertain and subject to debate. Consequently, a thorough understanding of this asymmetry at the EIC will be crucial in refining our understanding of the relevant wave functions and ultimately informing theoretical improvements in heavy-quark phenomenology. Furthermore, we establish that the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function can also be probed through the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production within deep central production, a process that is predominantly governed by the helicity distribution $g_1$ but with an interference contribution from the Sivers function. This leads to the formation of two separate combinations of asymmetries that enable us to disentangle the interference terms involving the dihadron fragmentation function and the Sivers function, respectively. This distinction allows us to precisely determine the dihadron fragmentation function's contribution and, in doing so, establish a crucial theoretical connection that further solidifies the importance of thorough understanding this asymmetry at the EIC. This understanding will ultimately facilitate accurate interpretations of data that will likely reveal the function's signs, a landmark discovery that would significantly contribute to the knowledge gained from the EIC in its initial phase of operation. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. This theoretical framework was later validated by Francis Murnaghan's formula, which provides a precise count of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). This book summarizes Springer's findings and includes an appendix detailing the derivation of Murnaghan's formula. A notable contribution of this research is the identification of two primary factors that determine conjugacy classes within the symplectic group: the type of natural invariant subgroups and the structures of Hermitian forms. This research builds upon earlier work by Elie Cartan, who initially explored conjugacy classes within the classical groups. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. We share our technique with the community, and it is currently deployed at Yahoo! News, serving over 10 million daily page views. Additionally, our entity recommendations have been adopted by other Yahoo! applications and websites. We have open-sourced our recommendation framework on GitHub under the Apache License, where it is utilized by other companies and research institutions in the field of computer science. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our study is complementary to existing research on word2vec, offering a rich resource for researchers seeking to design innovative embedding models that can uncover hidden patterns in diverse distributions of term co-occurrences. Our implementation of a word2vec-based classifier for financial text also yields superior performance, demonstrating the practical utility of these models in real-world applications. Our analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of these models provides a valuable foundation for addressing fundamental research questions in NLP, NAE, and statistics. Our exploration of the limitations of these models in the context of financial text also raises crucial questions for researchers in the field. Our analysis of the Loughran-McDonald polarities using these models reveals an interesting phenomenon, where the embeddings of certain polarized words exhibit a gradient-like structure, gradually transitioning from positive to negative polarities. This result is particularly surprising for the negative polarities, as the model is trained to predict the context given a specific set of words, rather than the words given the context. Our analysis of the frequencies of these words within the training dataset holds the key to understanding this phenomenon, showing that the words with negative polarities exhibit a greater diversity in their context

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. By breaking down CRDT design into manageable components and providing available implementation resources, the RWF framework is poised to enable other developers to design and execute their own CRDTs with ease. As we demonstrate Redis-RWF, our implementation of RWF using Redis, can be utilised as a utility to create Redis CRDTs. By leveraging Redis functions as part of the Redis ecosystem, Redis-RWF provides a versatile and efficient platform for developing new CRDTs. As we explore the possibilities of scaling Redis-RWF horizontally, our design framework is positionned to be highly adaptable and suitable for various distributed storage systems. With Redis-RWF, creating new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently is now achievable, and we anticipate that it will become a valuable resource for developers and researchers in the field of distributed storage. Through our work on Redis-RWF, we also demonstrate the design principles that can be employed to develop new data types with conflict resolution capabilities, and these design principles, in conjunction with the RWF framework, will facilitate the creation of additional CRDTs in the future. As we discuss the design principles that underpin Redis-RWF, its key components also serve as a case study for elevating the understanding of conflict-free replication techniques that can be applied to other data types. By exploring the possibilities of applying these design principles to other data types, Redis-RWF will continue to serve as an exemplar of a sophisticated CRDT in the field of distributed storage. With its flexible architecture that allows for horizontal scaling, Redis-RWF has established a new benchmark for what a sophisticated CRDT should strive to achieve. As we highlight the challenges that we encountered while designing and developing Redis-RWF, our work will also serve as a reference point for other developers who endeavour to create complex CRDTs in the future

We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics.
The solution also highlights the significant difference in wave energy preservation
at large radii between head and tail shocks, with a potential greater impact on
matter ejection. This distinction emphasizes the importance of waveforms in
shock evolution.
We also predict shock behavior during passages through spherical envelopes and
derive a heuristic formula for mass loss in response to internal shocks, which
could significantly contribute to mass loss in certain scenarios. Notably, our
predictions indicate that super-Eddington outbursts may result in the formation
of long-lived, low-amplitude shockwaves just beyond the stellar surface, which
could then interact with the host galaxy's interstellar medium, potentially
affecting the surrounding environment in shock front scenarios. We explore the
possibility of detecting these shocks through the light curves and radial
velocity curves of stars experiencing outbursts, which could provide a high-speed
camera view of shock behavior during these events. Additionally, we suggest
that certain Type II supernovae with extended envelopes may be the outcome of
this specific process, which could also result in the formation of astrophysical
multijet engines, such as those associated with some gamma-ray bursts, by
generating and focusing shocks within a massive, high-density ring layer just
before the star's collapse. We derive a criterion for identifying these stars
experiencing outbursts on the verge of collapse by comparing the shock energy to
the energy released from the star's collapse, which sets the stage for a more
in-depth analysis of these processes in future research. We also propose a new
framework for modeling and simulating shock behavior within flowing stars and
the potential for their magnetic axes to shift, resulting in changes to the
orientation of the beamed radiation, which could become misaligned with the
observer's view, leading to a decrease in the observed energy through a decrease

By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling with spin-orbit interaction, and the interaction of the centrifugal field with the crystal field with spin-orbit coupling. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects that had shed mass due to spinning and those that had not. Additionally, we found that the limits within which hydrogen burning stars formed depended on the density of the star rather than its mass. This was seen in the specific case of a 0.09 solar mass hydrogen-burning star, which could maintain stable rotation up to 44% of its critical rotation rate without rupturing. Furthermore, we discovered that the limits within which hydrogen burning stars formed could also depend on the presence of a host object, as seen in the case of a 0.08 solar mass hydrogen-burning binary star, which could maintain stable rotation up to 60% of its critical rotation rate without rupturing, due to the stabilizing effect of being part of a binary system. Finally, we found that the limits within which hydrogen burning stars formed could also depend on how the star formed, as seen in the specific case of 0.08 solar mass hydrogen-burning stars, which could maintain stable rotation up to 55% of their critical rotation rate without rupturing, due to the stabilizing effect of how they formed.

Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. As a result, parallel algorithms are highly recommended for handling matrix-based applications. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. Additionally, we explored the application of this method to a multiple-task coordination problem in a network environment, demonstrating that it yields an efficient cooperative performance that approaches the ideal found through exhaustive search. This knowledge is then utilized in developing several insightful models, such as classifications, predictions, and scoring systems used in various industries, including our country's key sectors. Unfortunately, as we demonstrate, the privacy protections built into the federated learning process can be compromised, allowing us to disclose sensitive information about 100,000 individuals without being detected by the system. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. By applying these techniques in a structured way, we were able to sequence unordered events with accuracy rates of up to 52%, reduce the disparity between the performance of machines and that of humans by 20%, and achieve expertise that surpasses general knowledge by a margin of at least 5%. Our research introduces several novel ideas, including the concept of sequential-aware pretraining for multimodal data and a diverse range of challenging sequential reasoning tasks that can be used to evaluate the ability of machines to understand real-world procedures. Additionally, we gather substantial evidence that points to the importance of sequential information in understanding and accurately sequencing unordered events and procedural knowledge from multiple sources. This understanding can be applied to complex real-world tasks like planning and the execution of tasks that require temporal common sense and the incorporation of various forms of information. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. The findings indicate that the distribution follows a power law with a fixed exponent equal to twice the degree of the nearest neighbor in the network. This means that some network nodes have a particularly high impact when removed, leading to a significant increase in their criticality. Therefore, targeted immunization based on these high-criticality nodes can be an effective strategy to reduce the spread of malicious information in networks. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our method exhibits superior denoising capabilities when compared to state-of-the-art 3D face denoising methods. Our method's testing script utilizes the Florence dataset, while our training script utilizes the AFLW2000-3D dataset. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. Furthermore, an analysis of a linear regression model with time-varying parameters is also conducted, and the findings suggest that conventional techniques can yield superior performance, which raises interesting questions about potential weaknesses in modern over-parameterized models. The study's outcomes have important implications for the utilization of time series linear models in high-dimensional environments. The study's outcomes are verified through extensive simulations under realistic settings and data scenarios. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our research lays the ground for further exploration into how storage units' risk profiles can be modeled and their risk preferences managed, via mechanisms such as payment incentives, that could ultimately maximize the effectiveness of storage units in contributing to grid stability.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to execute reliable two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors. The interaction between two-electron valleys is highly sensitive to position, orientation, and electric fields, meaning precise control over these variables is essential to executing two-qubit operations with consistency. The study also highlights the importance of selecting a specific in-plane orientation and aligning the connection between the two donors along the <110> direction to achieve the strongest possible exchange interaction. Moreover, it was determined that an applied electric field can be utilized as a control mechanism to execute two-qubit operations in a manner equivalent to implementing precise positioning control. The research provides a foundation for further investigation into donor-based quantum processing and the development of robust, scalable quantum technologies. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model separates the carrier transfer processes into two distinct steps: first, a neutralization of a hole Landau level within the bulk, followed by the transfer of carriers to the neutral state at the edge of the quantum well. Strong support for this model is derived from magnetophotometry measurements, which show a sharp rise in the recombination radiation near the neutral point when the magnetic field is low. Researchers suggest employing high-order cumulants and factorial cumulants of conserved charges to investigate critical dynamics in heavy-ion collision experiments. A parametric representation of the 3D Ising model, which shares a universality class with Quantum Chromo-Dynamics, is used in this study to examine how the second to fourth-order cumulant values of the order parameter change with temperature, and regardless of an external magnetic field at the critical temperature, these normalized cumulant values are independent, resulting in a temperature fixed point. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations in finite systems confirm the existence of this fixed point at temperatures near the critical point. The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD. This fixed point's existence in both models suggests it could be exploited to determine the critical temperature in experiments. Additionally, the behavior of these cumulants with magnetic field strength is investigated, and the discovery of a fixed point along the deconfinement transition line in the charge-order-parameter versus temperature plane could provide a key to interpreting the results of non-central heavy-ion collisions. The relationship between these cumulants and the order parameter's distribution is investigated by simulation, revealing that the fixed point arises due to the asymptotic behavior of this distribution as temperature decreases towards the critical point. This study also illustrates how the fixed point can be observed in experimental data if the order parameter's distribution is reweighted onto the standard, unlimited definition of cumulants. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding paves the way for further studies of heavy quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Additionally, the minimum-bias cross sectional measurement for top quark pairs at 8.16 TeV was found to be 60.3 microbarns with a 7.2 microbarns uncertainty, and was found to be rate-limited at low transverse momenta. This result holds significant potential for the study of heavy quark interactions with glouns in proton-nucleus collisions. Furthermore, a minimum bias event shape quantity known as the sum of the squares of the transverse momenta of all jets was measured and found to be consistent with theoretical models that account for medium response and jet phasing. This quantity showed no significant dependence on centrality or beam direction. A newly developed four-dimensional weighted sum method was used for the first time on heavy-ion data and was found to be effective in reducing systematic uncertainties and improving precision. This new method could be useful for extracting low-pT cross section information in future large-systematic-uncertainty experiments. Furthermore, the study of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions may provide valuable insights into heavy quark behavior in nuclear environments and the potential for heavy quark matter to exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. This study marks the first time top quark production has been detected and analyzed in proton-nucleus collisions. 

However, further investigation is needed to fully comprehend the implications of these findings on heavy quark behavior in nuclear environments. This study marks an important milestone in the development of top quark production analysis in proton-nucleus collisions and sets the stage for more in-depth investigations of heavy quark production and the properties of heavy quark matter. This study provides a thorough examination of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions based on full data sets from the CMS
