Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. We also derive the minimum required specifications for an IRS unit to achieve optimized target parameter estimation in the presence of noise. Furthermore, we examine the impact of various radar system parameters on target parameter estimation and provide a quantitative analysis of the optimal target reflection intensity. We also explore the effect of various radar system parameters on target parameter estimation in such scenarios. Lastly, we outline the results of this research and the obtained conclusions, in addition to suggesting potential future research directions focusing on multipath scenarios, diverse target shapes, and real-world implementations. With these potential advancements, the effectiveness of IRS technology can be further assessed across a wide range of radar applications. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. The introduced evaluation framework is available online for users to add their own fuzzers and testing subjects for evaluation purposes. In addition to presenting the evaluation results, this paper discusses the implications of its findings for the design of modern fuzzers. Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings, without assuming any particular structure in the game itself. Nonetheless, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of their method in relation to the number of queries made to the game itself. In our research, we establish a lower bound limiting the complexity of their approach by formulating a particular $\lambda$-Lipschitz game in a broad context of multi-action games, thereby setting a baseline for future advancements in this area. This breakthrough is particularly notable in the realm of one-action games, where our method for determining $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria requires a quantity of queries that scales exponentially with the ratio of $\epsilon$ to $\lambda$, thus marking an uncompromising departure from the known subexponential query complexities in non-Lipschitz games. Our findings are further validated by a theoretical analysis as well as extensive empirical data, where our algorithm for finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in multi-action $\lambda$-Lipschitz games exhibits a query complexity that is distinctively characteristic of games where one action serves as a dominant strategy. In such games, the complexity is defined by a query complexity that scales polynomially with the ratio of $\epsilon$ to $\lambda$, thereby facilitating a critical insight into the underlying reasons responsible for delayed convergence in the presence of competition. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. In addition, by examining the relationship between stress and the activated volume at different levels of confinement, scientists have obtained stress and fraction volume phase diagrams for both anisotropic and shear-induced jamming, providing a comprehensive framework that is both universally applicable and potentially relevant to other complex systems.

A specific member of this family, denoted as $Z_4(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, is then examined in detail. A generator set for this algebra is determined and analyzed in the context of the Hilbert-Poincaré series, and a corresponding polynomial is derived to describe its dimensional structure. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Originally presented at the 2020 IEEE American Control Conference, this work is now being freely shared due to the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on global research collaboration. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This novel algorithm also converges to the same outcome as the Monte Carlo method but does so in seconds rather than minutes. A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Ultimately, all data and calculation tools are made available for researchers to explore these phenomena further or uncover new insights. 

This dataset originated from the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Review of Marine Transport Statistics compiled by renowned shipping experts, former CEOs, and key industry figures. Valuable information about ship classification, shipping routes, and the conversion of shipping units into actual container units can also be found in the provided documentation. 

Originally compiled by Professor Jan Anderberg, this dataset has been thoroughly reviewed and corrected with input from multiple shipping industry experts. Their input ensured the accuracy of the data, especially around the periods of 1966 to 1970 and 1980 to 1982 which were prone to reporting errors. Anderberg collaborated with these experts to validate the data against actual market events such as the dramatic shift in market share that occurred during the 1960s when Asian countries began to compete globally or the significant oil price increases in 1973 and 1979. 

In the UNCTAD data, freight rates are expressed in US dollars per unit of cargo, shipping quantity is measured in units of cargo per month, new ship prices and used ship prices are presented in US dollars, and scrap ship prices are shown as a percentage of a new ship's price.

This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries. This achievement permits us to establish a global version of the Schoen-Yau theorem, which connects the conformal deformation of compact, singular areas with the fundamental group of the underlying space. This global framework theorem, in turn, enables us to prove the existence of a conformal metric of positive scalar curvature on a wide range of manifolds, including those with singularities along their boundary components. This conclusion generalizes earlier results from a previous study. Additionally, we are able to demonstrate that the minimal geometries associated with the conformal deformations described in Part I contain a Lorentzian component, which results from the analysis of their tangent cones. This analysis further reveals the presence of a non-compact, singular hyper surface within these geometries, allowing us to establish a relationship between its fundamental group and the geometry of the associated cone. This connection enables us to prove the existence of a conformal metric of positive scalar curvature on a variety of manifolds defined by graph constructions, which include those described by Peo. This achievement expands upon earlier outcomes from a previous investigation. Lastly, we also establish the existence of a conformal metric of positive scalar curvature on manifolds featuring singularities resembling the Boucci example. This conclusion generalizes results from a previous study. Nonetheless, we do note that the Manfredi example is compatible with the Yamabe flow. This reevaluation leads us to realize that our earlier approaches to conformally deforming minimal geometries, while unique, can still be improved. This improvement results in a more streamlined proof of our main conclusion in Part II. This revised proof relies on a key observation about the properties of the associated tangent cones, which allows us to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries. A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that induces a thermal gradient. This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy ratio in the vortex liquid, which in terms of units $\frac{\hbar}{k_B}$, is much greater than what is typically found in common liquids. Moreover, there's a distinction to be made between the entropy held within the vortex core and the entropy bound to a moving magnetic flux line. A crucial aspect to consider here is that the entropy within the vortex core undergoes a continuous exchange with the surrounding normal quasi-particles due to a normal steady flow, which causes a decrease in the entropy bound within the core as the vortex moves at a slower speed. A vortex will eventually release all the entropy bound within its core within a specific distance, which is on the order of the coherence length of the superconducting material. This will occur provided that the ratio between the energy gap and the Fermi energy is sufficiently large. A comparison between this entropy binding energy, which is on the order of meV and dependent on the type of superconducting material, and the other energetic components that a vortex may possess is also presented in this study. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Additionally, we explore the incorporation of MEF in broader online optimization frameworks, such as the generalized unadjusted and adjusted algorithms, and investigate what parameters can be set in an offline setting to achieve optimal flexibility, leading to further cost reductions. This enables a practical and flexible implementation of our feedback mechanism in real-world applications. A key parameter in our results is the discount factor, and under certain conditions, we establish the optimal policy as a result of rigorous numerical analysis, to guide the selection of future weights in our online optimization process. A major aspect of our study is the inclusion of a Markov Decision Process case, where we derive policy-dependent variance, prove the convergence of our self-tuning variable step-size REINFORCE, and show the results of our experiments on a solar forecasting dataset, resulting in an adaptation that yields an order of magnitude better than fixed-step-size methods, and highlight the use of our public dataset, comprising approximately one million data points, obtained from approximately 7000 unique users, providing valuable insights into the behavior of electric vehicles in California from 2014 to2015. A key aspect of our research is the creation of an open-source Python framework, referred to as the online learning framework, and an accompanying charging-specific application program interface, available for download from our public repository. A detailed examination of the challenges facing the integration of more accurate weather forecasts, particularly forecasting the wind, is also presented, and a glimpse into our ongoing research, centered on the proposal of a new MEF variant, is given. To circumvent this issue, researchers use numerical simulations, often in the form of 1D and 2D models, to create a range of possible CE behaviors and compare them with theoretical predictions, known as the SCATTER code. By combining multiple simulations, the code produces a standardized set of CE rules, which can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including interactions between stars and the expulsion of matter during mergers. This approach helps to clarify the underlying mechanics of the CE process and may provide insights that could be applied to other merger-related phenomena. Our study shows that at the energy and luminosity planned for CLIC, the nuisance of the heavy Higgs boson and most BSM Higgs couplings will be well constrained, while at ILC energies, BSM signatures in double Higgs production will be detectable for significantly heavier masses. Additionally, we investigate the feasibility of studying the heavy Higgs boson and BSM Higgs couplings through double Higgs production at these colliders, ultimately finding that this process offers the most sensitive testing of the Higgs sector at these electron-positron colliders. Lastly, we determine the required energies and luminosities for full BSM sensitivity in double Higgs production across the two collider types.

The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. A method was proposed for calculating the anisotropy of objects with irregular shapes, like blocks and plates. This research could be relevant to swimmers, like turtles and fish, that move quickly through sediment on the ocean floor. This drag anisotropy may also explain the way some animals, like the sandfish lizard, move efficiently through sand by swinging their whole bodies. This study uses a combination of direct observation and mathematical modeling to understand the drag anisotropy of objects moving through granular beds.

Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. Furthermore, our research showcases that expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure is valuable resources that, when leveraged, can accelerate the auto-tuning process. With the expertise incorporated into the model, BoAnon-generated configurations perform similarly to those produced by system experts. This consistency holds true across different evaluation criteria, resulting in optimized configurations that also exhibit better performance in terms of energy consumption. By incorporating the structure of the system into the optimization process, BoAnon is able to produce efficient configurations that are both effective and efficient, achieving a 4-6x factor improvement in energy-latency objectives. Although this technique accelerates the auto-tuning process, the generated configurations are specific to the log data used during training. As a result, BoAnon faces challenges when adapting to new hardware, requiring a more comprehensive understanding of the system's structure and performance models. To overcome these difficulties, researchers are currently exploring ways to enhance the structure learning component of BoAnon, such that the algorithm can discover the system's structure and performance models from logs in a more efficient and effective manner. This research direction, although still in its infancy, is a critical step in further accelerating the auto-tuning process and enabling BoAnon to handle a broader range of computer systems with many parameters. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Notably, we observed $v_3$ to be driven by the interaction between quarks and gluons in mid-central Au+Au collisions. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  In a comparison study with four other quality assessment techniques, our proposed solution has shown significant performance gains, achieving speed-ups of up to 7.5 times in data quality assessment tasks.  The source code of DistQualityAssessment is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/sansainc/DistQualityAssessment.  This system has further been deployed on a cloud platform available at https://data.anc.org/. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. Additionally, it investigates $B^0_s \to \tau^+\tau^-$ decays at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of approximately 3 inverse femtometers. A thorough review of the available data from the ATLAS collaboration up to April 2019 is provided in this study. Concurrently, it also includes an overview of the ATLAS detector's configuration used for these measurements and a brief description of the key production mechanisms of beauty mesons. Furthermore, this study outlines the theoretical framework and key variables employed in these experiments. It also illustrates the deployment of mock data by means of likelihood ratios and employs a notation where the first notation represents the initial beauty meson, the second notation represents the secondary particle, and the third notation represents the specific decay mode. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. The model's code and dataset are made available to the research community. As the training process relies on vast collections of images rather than underlying traffic patterns, SceneGen faces the challenge of parameterization. While it excels at inserting multiple virtual characters into the environment, further refinement is needed to control the scenario's overall composition. As a result, scene generation is primarily confined to single-lane roads. Further development is needed to broaden its applicability to more complex road environments. Nevertheless, SceneGen offers significant advancements in the generation of realistic traffic scenarios. Furthermore, when combined with motion planning and control models, the potential exists for SceneGen to train end-to-end autonomous vehicle systems through simulation. Through the creation of realistic simulation environments, SceneGen enables the thorough evaluation of high-risk scenarios that would be impractical and unsafe to conduct in real-world settings. These measures, not previously identified, serve as periodic components within the model's phase diagram. We demonstrate that they comply with the principles of a Grassmannian representation, and may only exist when the model's parameters fall within a specific range that forms an irrational angle with the x-axis. These measures exhibit distinct temperatures, exhibiting a thermodynamic phase transition at $-\log\tan\theta$. Additionally, we establish that they are associated with index-2 subgroups within the model's duality symmetry. These periodic measures can also be understood through the lens of a Galois connection, particularly within an interval that forms an irrational multiple with the x-axis. Here, we establish a connection between the model's periodic measures and its symmetric breaking. Finally, we investigate how these measures can be linked to the model's periodic boundary conditions, and show that they can be combined to result in a periodic measure that is linked to an index-4 normal subgroup within the model's duality symmetry. These findings provide a basis for exploring more complex lattice structures. Indeed, we provide a theorem stating that any periodic measure present on a Cayley tree can be transferred to a product measure within a higher-dimensional lattice. This theorem holds significant implications for the model's self-duality and its critical behavior, and may be used to investigate more complex lattice structures. Additionally, we discuss how these measures can be combined with the model's boundary conditions, and show that they can be linked to the model's periodic component within its Hamiltonian. This connection enables us to re-examine the model's phase transition, and provide a more in-depth analysis of its thermodynamic behavior. This analysis reveals a more complex critical surface, and shows that the model's critical transition can occur through multiple pathways. Furthermore, we investigate how these measures can be linked to the model's symmetry under a higher order operator, and show that they can be combined to result in a periodic component within the model's self-energy. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, the article derives a theoretical convergence rate of $O(\tau +h^2)$ for a specific conservative system, and showcases the method's efficiency and effectiveness by applying it to a dissipative nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The proposed iteration method offers a viable alternative to traditional implicit time-stepping methods for discretization techniques that ensure property preservation. The method's implementation details, including its computational cost, are explicitly outlined, making it an appealing option for preserving discrete properties while resolving nonlinear systems via iterative methods. The study also explores the behavior of multiple variants of the iteration method, even enhancing one variant to enforce additional constraints, thereby further establishing its utility across a broader class of preservation-based discretization techniques. The article's findings are further verified using a publicly available reference solution, and all proposed variants outperform their explicit counterparts in terms of computational cost. The method's potential advantages and possible future research directions along with various preservation-based discretization techniques, as well as our current implementation of the iteration method in Python, are also made available for public use. The method's code is currently compatible with the FEniCS Project but is designed in a way that allows it to be integrated with any Python-based finite element framework. The reference solution, all variants of the iteration method, and our Python implementation of the method are all available for download at the provided URL. The code's design follows the established best practices for Python packages, and is also easily adaptable to other preservation-based discretization techniques. The study's findings provide a viable solution to the widespread use of structure-preserving approximations of time-dependent partial differential equations, and the proposed iteration method is suitable for any preservation-based discretization technique that is conservative or dissipative. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been defined clearly and there is no widely-accepted evaluation standard. To address this issue, we created Far3D, a leading evaluation standard that defines far-field detection as identifying 30% of medium-size objects more than 25m away from the sensor, or 20% of large objects more than 50m away. We also introduced a new benchmark called Far3D-Retrieval, which involves finding distant objects across far-field ranges or beyond, plus we discovered that enhancing three-dimensional detection models using distillation also significantly improves their performance on the Far3D standard, a finding that we showed through extensive experiments using the Far3D-Retrieval benchmark. Our project code is available at https://github.com/ShangxiaoHuang/Far3Det. Our research paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04918. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action. A discussion on the issues related to scalability of the current approach and the potential of circuit-based quantum machine learning to revolutionize the field of chemistry also follows and several suggestions given on how to overcome these challenges domestically. A thorough analysis on the applications of this approach to composite systems that has been theorized follows in the latter part of this article. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently register unknown intraoperative surfaces with preoperative volume models during real-time applications. Experimental results show that this approach yields superior performance when compared with traditional methods in terms of precision and speed. The implementation of this algorithm using CUDA and MATLAB allows for real-time processing. The source code is available for public use at https://github.com/ghsmrgh/3DRegistration. The evaluation of the algorithm was conducted using simulated data, yet it has also been successfully demonstrated with actual liver tissue during real-time liver surgery simulation. The recently developed datasets W-LSS17 and W-LSS18 for weakly supervised liver segmentation are also presented. These datasets consist of easily accessible, unlabeled intraoperative surfaces from 17 and 18 patients, respectively, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/ghsmrgh/WeaklySupervisedLiverSegmentation. These datasets along with our algorithm represent a significant step forward in solving the non-rigid registration problem, particularly in real-time applications. The unique approach of the deep learning-based algorithm, where a single network trains the unseen data and achieves superior performance, is a groundbreaking achievement. This is further accentuated by the fact that this type of data usually cannot be obtained in organ surgery scenarios. Furthermore, the introduction of the W-LSS17, W-LSS18 datasets, along with our top-performing algorithm code, will serve as a benchmark for any new methods developed in the field of weakly-supervised 3D registration. The high degree of difficulty associated with this problem has been incorrectly attributed to misalignment issues; instead, the primary source of difficulty lies in accurately modeling the biomechanical properties of organs. A novel approach to resolving this issue is presented in this paper, where the unknown variables, such as boundary conditions and organ properties, are treated as part of the surface correspondence problem. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. Our findings show that these hybrid networks offer accurate classification results across multiple datasets, also demonstrating that they can achieve comparable performance to traditional neural networks with significantly reduced parameters. Furthermore, we illustrate that these hybrid networks can achieve substantial energy savings during actual classification operations, a critical consideration for the long-term viability of deploying such models across multiple platforms. Our implementation is straightforward and easily integrable into popular deep learning frameworks, making our proposal highly suitable for real-world application scenarios. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Our findings indicate that the mass-thickness curve of spin-polarized strange quark stars depends significantly on the interplay between the magnetic field and temperature, displaying two possible mass ranges. Additionally, we discovered that temperature has a diminishing effect on the maximum mass-thickness curve of spin-polarized strange quark stars, whereas the effect of the magnetic field is one of enhancement. Our model also facilitates comparison with observational data through the use of model parameters, and we demonstrate that spin-polarized strange quark stars may exhibit considerable temperatures, potentially exceeding 50 MeV. The model is versatile enough to account for magnetic field influences on quark matter properties within various magnetic field strengths, which may prove useful in interpreting astronomical data. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of spin-polarized strange quark star structure, including predictions on quark star radius, the temperature and magnetic field dependence of mass-thickness curves, and possible identifications of spin-polarized strange quark stars through X-ray satellite observations. Furthermore, we propose a method for identifying spin-polarized strange quark stars with temperatures below the gluon condensate critical temperature, which may also present as color superconducting quark stars. Our study also highlights the importance of distinguishing spin-polarized strange and non-spin-polarized strange quark stars in order to accurately interpret astronomical data, which could provide valuable insights into the composition and properties of strange matter. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Our findings contribute a new method to create E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, involving the combination of a papillon graph and a bipartite cubic graph connected by an edge. Finally, our work concludes with an observation regarding edge-colourings in these graphs. A related Hamiltonian-related property, called the Hamiltonian-edge-invariant property, is also defined and some of its related results are some of its related results are also presented with respect to the papillon graph family. Our approach to studying these properties involves an analysis of their relationships with perfect matchings, Hamiltonian cycles and edge-colourings in the papillon graph and its derivatives. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies common issues associated with static analysis techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters that cover all possible scenarios a program may encounter, and the generation of filters that are too large for memory to process. Furthermore, Timeloops offers enhanced security by analyzing each system call made by a program at a individual level rather than relying on the characteristics of the program as a whole. Development of Timeloops involved the creation of a new analysis technology called Time-constant Data Structure (TCS) policy learning, a method for creating Timeloops, and a new execution engine called Time-dependent Data Structure (TDS) policy enforcement. A multi-tool approach was utilized to build and test Timeloops for use with applications developed with the Haxe language and also for existing microservices built with various programming languages and frameworks, such as Java, C++, and.NET. Experimental evaluations demonstrated that Timeloops poses minimal performance overhead and successfully blocked all unauthorized system calls made by programs in our test suite, even when subjected to diverse input data. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. By applying these strategies to synthetic data scenarios, both WRI and ESI are successfully implemented and their outcomes are compared with those of FWI. The results show that all three methods can produce comparable images when using high-quality data, but with the use of noisy data, time-domain ESI delivers the best seismic imaging performance.  Finally, the implications of these developments and potential pathways for resolving the storage issue with time-domain wavefields are considered.  To overcome this limitation, a hybrid approach is proposed, utilizing frequency-domain data for layered backgrounds and time-domain data for structural complexities, and this has significant cost and storage benefits, suggesting this could be a highly effective tool for seismic imaging in complex geological settings. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. Furthermore, we present a method for calculating the flux of cosmic neutrons and utilize this approach to report the observed neutron flux as a function of muon energy and scattering angle. The data collected indicate the observed neutrons result from the interaction of cosmic muons with 568 meters of water equivalent in depth, assuming a muon energy spectrum following a $E^{-2.1}$ form. Moreover, we explore the capability of this apparatus to analyze the composition of rock beneath the laboratory and, with some upgrades, it has the potential to examine the neutron production associated with ultra-high energy cosmic particles. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS target list is representative of the broader population of planets identified by TESS, and our automated targeting approach can efficiently identify suitable candidates from the vast dataset produced by TESS. The details of our targeting framework can be applied to other similar surveys, such as OREOS and SCExES-KECK. For the complete TKS dataset, our analysis reveals that the radii of the target planets cover a broad range, likely consisting of low-core-mass planets, and that the targets with the highest priority for follow-up observations with JWST are likely to be planets with compositions similar to those of Neptune. The effectiveness of our targeting algorithm in pinpointing suitable candidates for observational data is demonstrated by our analysis of the final TKS dataset, and we provide the details of our approach for incorporating the properties of the host stars into the target selection process. This incorporates the facts that the stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities, and that the targets with the highest priority for follow-up observations with JWST are likely to be planets with compositions similar to those of Neptune. The diverse characteristics of the TKS targets, particularly regarding the planets' dynamical configurations and their compositions, will ultimately enable our investigation of how these properties are linked to the characteristics of their host stars. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this force, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this phenomenon, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Through this research, it became clear that the YORP effect plays a crucial role in starting the rotational acceleration of asteroids by providing a net torque that results from the interaction between solar radiation and the asteroid's surface. Additionally, this study implies the presence of a non-symmetric mass distribution in three detected cases, as well as the presence of the solar precession feature in two instances, which could serve as a potential means of predicting future light curve minima and maxima. By using this analysis, the rotation period of these three asteroids is expected to increase beyond one day in the year 2080 and in the year 2175 for Toro and Geographos, respectively. Furthermore, this study highlights the significance of obtaining multiple transit observations and further data through both photometric and radar techniques in order to better comprehend the rotational states of small asteroids. Through this research it is also clear that the YORP effect possesses sufficient energy to change an asteroid's spin state and shape over time, which could in turn increase the chances of an asteroid breaking apart due to its rapid rotation. As a result of this acceleration, material on the equatorial region of an asteroid could be ejected into space, creating a ring system, or other smaller asteroids, thus making the YORP effect a crucial feature that needs further study in order to comprehend the origin of smaller asteroids in our solar system.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This disproves a previous conjecture linking topological compactness to compactness within the surface's interior for such groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that groups of this type, whose points of accumulation do not lie on the boundary, are not topologically compact. This proof relies on categorizing homeomorphisms based on their boundary behavior and establishing that certain subgroups act freely within a larger family of surfaces, thereby connecting this action to abundant discrete actions on the real line. This, in turn, allows us to derive additional information about these subgroups' properties. Finally, we establish that certain subgroups of homeomorphisms with boundary behavior classified as 'Anosov' are non-compact when using a specific topology, and that this non-compactness arises from a combination of factors including vast discrete actions on the real line, vast discrete actions within families of hyperbolic surfaces, and abundant discrete actions within families of tori. This result may be generalized to a broader class of groups, including those consisting of surface homeomorphisms with boundary behavior classified as 'pseudo-Anosov'. This non-compactness of these groups has significant implications for the Roelcke precompactness of these groups, and ultimately leads to the conclusion that vast subgroups of surface homeomorphisms with boundary behavior classified as 'Anosov' or 'pseudo-Anosov' do not have compact action within the surface's interior. This conclusion holds under the assumption that Richard Lyons' theorem holds true. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework is utilized to analyze a sample of 43 M-dwarfs from the Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample, and the resulting properties are validated through cross-checks of the data. The temperature measurements are further verified by matching the optical and near-infrared color predictions to the observed values, confirming the validity of the temperature findings. The newly calculated mass and radius values for the M-dwarfs in the sample are also compared to previous study outcomes. The precision of the temperature measurements can vary depending on the specific UV spectral features used, with a uniform most likely value of $3793\pm 100$ K for the average temperature of the sample, while the mass and radius estimates display a greater level of variation, with an average mass of $0.476\pm 0.036 M_\odot$ and an average radius of $0.486\pm 0.022 R_\odot$. The outcomes of this research provide a solid foundation for the follow-up studies in this series, specifically the analysis of ionization that will be presented in paper II. The ultraviolet spectral features of the M-dwarfs in the sample are found to be largely unaffected by ionization, although there is some evidence that the ionized state may have a more significant impact on larger and more active stars. This, however, can be further explored using the extensive data set of field M-dwarfs, and the detailed stellar properties calculated in this study. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that maintain the same value for similar input strings. With this characterization, a wide class of continuous functions can be proven computable, including those defined by deterministic finite-state machines with specific properties, such as being deterministic, finite-state machines with lookup tables, and even certain types of recursive functions, such as the unbounded version of the counter function. 

Additionally, a method is devised to create a corresponding Turing machine for any computable function, although this approach relies on the ability to select individual letters from an infinite input stream, a capability that is itself an open question. On the negative side, a counterexample is provided to show that not all computable functions can be defined by finite-state machines, even when allowing for two passes through the input. 

Finally, based on the proposed characterization of computable functions, a new algorithm is developed to decide if a given transducer is computable and, if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine, albeit one with additional privileges to select individual letters from an infinite input stream. This new algorithm combines previous results with new insights, leading to a more efficient decision-making approach, although one that is still not feasible with just a single pass through the input. 

On the theoretical side, the proposed characterization of computable functions leads to a deeper understanding of the underlying principles and can be applied to other related problems, such as determining if a given function is decidable and, if so, creating a corresponding Turing machine, as well as deciding if a given function preserves a specific property over similar input strings. Furthermore, this characterization can also be used to create new types of transducers, such as prefix-dependent transducers, that can be computed efficiently.

Furthermore, this difference in longitudinal polarization was utilized to determine the branching fraction of the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons. The resulting branching fraction values for both the $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ decays to a pair of $K^*$ mesons are as follows: for $B^0$, the value is $0.210 \pm 0.008 \pm 0.011 \pm 0.001$, and for $B^0_s$, the value is $0.119 \pm 0.007 \pm 0.006 \pm 0.001$. The given errors stem from statistical, systematic, and radiative corrections in the case of $B^0$ decay branchling fraction measurement. Additionally, an upper limit for the branching fraction of the $B^+\to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decay was established at $0.0062$ at a $95\%$ confidence level. The resulting properties for the $B^0_S \to K^* \overline{K}^*$ decay amplitude distribution were also determined in this study, and these properties will be useful in distinguishing this decay from the $B^0 \to K^* \overline{K}^*$ decay in the presence of radiative corrections. 

Researchers at the CERN collider have successfully determined the difference in the longitudinal polarization of two specific mesons, and this discovery, coupled with the fact that time-dependent $CP$ violation analysis is not feasible due to the rapid $K^* \overline{K}^*$ decay rate, has motivated a new approach to understanding these decays. This approach entails a time-integrated study of two-body decay events, and through this study, the branchling fraction of one of these decays was measured for the first time. Furthermore, this new approach enables researchers to differentiate between two closely related meson decays, and this differentiation has the potential to enhance our understanding of these decays as well as certain key variables in these decays.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've also introduced a Cauchy-type variant of this approach, which uses an initial guess that can be obtained through a related but less complex analysis, and has shown that this variant converges to the solution of the original Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. This method is particularly well-suited for problems involving high-dimensional state spaces that can be processed efficiently by a distributed batch computation. We've tested this algorithm on a smooth model of a rotating disk, for which we've derived a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, and have demonstrated its effectiveness in finding the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he posed the question whether the corrected formula for $x$ given $y \ge (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ would continue to hold for values of $x$ derived from the formula itself, which we also confirm to be true for 64-bit computers. 

We also discuss how this more general formula can be implemented to improve the performance of factoring algorithms, such as the General Number Field Algorithm, by selectively focusing on smaller integers. 

Finally, we examine the implications of our discoveries on the distribution of prime powers, which follows a pattern of $x^{1/2} \rho(1/2) + x^{1/3} \rho(1/3) + \ldots$ for large values of x, assuming the RH. 

We also prove that the generalized logarithm function used in previous work can be replaced by a direct derivative of the Dickman function. 

We derive a formula that gives the count of $x$ for any value of the Dickman function $\rho(y)$.

Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We introduce a novel loss function variation that we term "balanced loss," capable of adapting to optimal performance parameters, demonstrating a 2.5% improvement in average precision across three diverse benchmark datasets, including the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST datasets. Notably, this improvement is akin to the gains derived from employing data augmentation, yet achieved without incorporating additional training data. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we develop a unified meta-algorithm that can leverage any online feedback type, thereby allowing it to work with a diverse range of teacher feedback. By doing so, we significantly expand the possibilities of learning from feedback in robotics, as it enables the use of feedback types that were previously inaccessible. Our proposed framework is flexible enough to incorporate any reinforcement learning (RL) solver and any type of online feedback, proving its own RL computability. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the learning of complex household navigation tasks on a robotic platform, highlighting its capacity to efficiently learn from a variety of noisy feedback. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/path-rl/path-learn-from-feedback. This study delves into the implications of these discoveries for the formation of colliding black-hole - neutron-star binaries, including a notable candidate such as GW190426_152155 reported in the second Gravitational Wave Catalogue. Furthermore, it examines the influence of birth velocities and neutron star sizes on the generation of such systems, along with any potential electromagnetic counterparts associated with them. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  The model's code is available for public access at https://github.com/wh1573356/ClosingTheLoop.  The research further showcases multiple rain elimination models in video demonstrations available at https://youtube.youtube/shorts/VT2fOOFwPOA and https://youtube.youtube/shorts/8QD05Dn-an4.  The paper is published in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing volume 29, 2020.  An extended version of the paper is also published in arXiv preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.06780 in 2020.  The authors of the paper received the IEEE Access Best Paper Award in 2021.  Moreover, a study based on the paper was published in Applied Sciences in 2021.  Another research project related to the paper was published in Journal of Intelligent Information Systems in 2021.  One more study related to the paper was published in Software: Practice and Technology in 2022.  Additionally, a project based on the paper was published in Journal of Supercomputing in 2022.  A related study to the paper was published in Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience in 2022.  One more paper related to Closing The Loop algorithm was published in Future Generation Computer Systems in 2023.

Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Although some argue that this axiom of completeness is flawed due to the counterexample provided by the Robinson quantifier, we present additional theories where the dependency holds robustly. Ultimately, the coexistence of distinct models with respect to the Continuum problem can be understood as resulting from the lack of a recursive axiom set for set theory, as demonstrated by a computability theoretic analysis.
