Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. The research found that personality traits, particularly neuroticism and conscientiousness, played a significant role in predicting drug consumption, while impulsivity and sensation seeking provided significant but less significant predictions for certain substances. The effect of withdrawing features, such as impulsivity and sensation seeking, resulted in a notable decrease in prediction accuracy only for the ecstasy cluster, indicating that other features took over as key predictors. The precision of the models was confirmed through a cross-validation technique, ensuring the consistency of the results, and the models performed notably better than a baseline classifier. The research used a diverse range of online surveys, gathering data from over 21,000 participants, aged between 18 and 46, from diverse backgrounds. The data analysis indicated that the classification accuracy dropped by only three percent when evaluating the accuracy with data from the same group that was used for training the models. Notably, the accuracy increased to over 75 percent for the ecstasy cluster when evaluating with data from a different group. The research provides insights into the characteristics that define safe and high-risk consumption patterns for different drugs, offering a starting point for developing targeted early intervention programs. The study suggests that programs aimed at reducing the risk of safe drug consumption should focus on individuals with a conscientious and low neurotic personality. On the other hand, programs aimed at reducing high-risk consumption patterns should target individuals with a neurotic and impulsive personality. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. Its implementation is available via the Q# based code library known as OpenFinance, an open-source framework for Finance that is currently hosted on GitHub. Through the utilization of a real-world scenario comprising up to 1000 stock prices, NISQ-HHL has shown the capability to generate high-quality portfolios, ultimately outperforming their classical counterparts in terms of portfolio returns while maintaining similar levels of risk. This is the first time the effectiveness of hybrid Quantum-Classical methods has been validated via actual market data. Furthermore, the implementation of these methods as code libraries will accelerate the exploration of actual use cases for Quantum computing within the realm of Finance. As a result, financial institutions can leverage these libraries to develop applications that can leverage the capabilities of both current and upcoming Quantum hardware. Alongside the attainment of better financial returns, applications of this kind have the potential to significantly showcase the value of Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware within the domain of Finance. Through the integration of actual quantum process characterizations, including amplitude decay and an average gate fidelity of 92.8%, this research furnishes a realistic framework for the development of practical Quantum applications. This research is the first to integrate the simulation of actual quantum process characterizations within the development of a practical Quantum application. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. Additionally, we obtain an rate bound for the first $k_n$ parking locations at a specific location, and a related maximum probability problem is also considered. This problem is then applied to obtain rate bounds for two extrema problems related to uniform random variables over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Lastly, this work extends previously known limits for the mean and the second raw moment of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Finally, an open problem is also presented in this paper. Additionally, we observe that the standard uniform distribution is a limit in probability distribution for the first $k_n$ parking locations, and we formally define a new sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with uniform conditional distributions. This new sequence is then shown to converge to a Poisson-Dirichlet distribution with a parameter of $1$, and this convergence is shown to result in the convergence of the first $k_n$ parking locations to a Poisson-Dirichlet distribution with the same parameter for a larger value of $k_n$. This conclusion provides a means to which we can apply thinning to obtain the limiting distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations. This limit is then shown to be equivalent to a known limit obtained through a different method, and it confirms the convergence of the first $k_n$ parking locations to a specific limit. This confirmation provides the basis for additional limit results derived in this paper. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection via unclonable encryption. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of possible copy-protection methods. Finally, we outline a novel construction based on entangled games, which can serve as a plug-in module for various copy-protection protocols. Our hope is that exploring unclonable encryption will yield novel mechanisms for secure multi-party computations and digital signatures with improved clonability-resistant properties. Our theory also facilitates a deeper understanding of quantum cryptography, encompassing topics such as monogamy of entanglement, non-interference, and randomness, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between these fundamental concepts and the unique aspects of quantum computation. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. This research is significant because it lays the groundwork for developing deep learning models capable of processing various types of low-dose PET scans across different applications, such as neurology and oncology, improving their reliability in clinical settings. Furthermore, this work facilitates further research into neural network architectures that can handle complex physical imaging processes and incorporate multiple imaging modalities. We also introduce an open-source Python framework that can generate various PET-MRI protocols for training and testing and make several key findings available, including several statistical tables. We provide comprehensive documentation on this framework, which can be adapted to develop uncertainty-aware deep learning models for other imaging applications. This framework is suitable for large-scale experiments and can be easily integrated into high-performance computing clusters using Python's distributed training functionality. We also introduce an open-source GitHub repository that can be used as a framework for developing deep learning models in image synthesis. We demonstrate the performance enhancements of this model over baseline deep learning architectures, such as style transfer and vanilla deep learning models, and show several examples of enhanced PET images alongside their corresponding MRI scans, as well as several out-of-distribution PET-MRI acquisitions. Additionally, we explore the reliability of this model in real-world settings, including its biologically-inspired design and potential applications. Our approach suggests a new way to view user data as a means to an end, rather than an end in itself. We achieve this by limiting data collection to absolute necessities required for a functional news experience. Furthermore, we introduce a theoretical framework that deems user data as a shared resource, subject to fair usage terms similar to those governing data usage in other contexts. We believe that viewing user data in this manner has far-reaching implications that can shape the future of the technology industry. We invite the research community to explore this perspective and contribute to a much-needed discussion on responsible data practices. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, our source-vertex parameterized algorithm is the first in a long line of parameterized algorithms to be proposed for the upward planarity problem. Our solutions are outlined in detail, including a general XP algorithm that uses a combination of SPQR tree-decompositions and bidirectional 2-way treewidth parameterized algorithms, leading to a time complexity of O(3^k * p(n)). We also describe a protocol for implicitly determining source vertices during an SPQR tree-decomposition, which enables our source-vertex parameterized algorithm to complete in O(4.38^k * p(n)) time. These results demonstrate the potential of combining parameterized techniques with decompositional approaches, yielding efficient solutions for graph layout problems, and highlighting the complexity of these problems when source vertices are present. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Moreover, this research indicates that beam breakup in multi-pass energy recovery linacs is highly sensitive to machine design, suggesting the usefulness of detailed studies in optimizing performance across various accelerator applications. The lessons learned from this study can also be applied to other types of accelerators, such as proton synchrotrons and heavy ion accelerators, where beam-RF interaction and beam breakup instability play a crucial role in determining achievable intensities. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is publicly available on https://github.com/eth-srl/ekmp. Additionally, we explore the formulation of our biodynamic bucket handling task as a nonlinear imitation learning problem, presenting a suite of 3D point cloud datasets available for public use at https://github.com/eth-srl/bdb3d-datasets. Our work lays the ground for extending linear kernelized movement primitives to nonlinear cases, and for developing constraints that can flexibly handle multiple hard constraints, such as overlapping obstacles, including the application of biodynamic objects with complex dynamics. Our work is also a step towards formulating obstacle avoidance in imitation learning, and for releasing publicly accessible 3D point cloud datasets suitable for robot learning. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. All results were verified against existing literature in relevant limits. In addition to contributing to an NNLL BFKL equation, the two-gluon CEV is expected to influence predictions made with colloid-like impact factor equations that have been successful in explaining observed characteristics of hadron fragmentation functions. In particular, this solution resolves an earlier issue with the sign of certain components of the photon fragmentation function within hadron structure data. Furthermore, this new understanding may also shed light on certain discrepancies within gluon distribution functions, although further analysis is needed to determine this fully. In contrast to colloid-like models, however, a distinct feature of the two-gluon CEV is its failure to adhere to a non-negative property required by such models, instead exhibiting a component that is negative in certain configurations. In light of these findings, the term 'colloid-like' can be defined more precisely as being equivalent to a two-gluon CEV that is positive in all configurations. In conclusion, despite being constrained to the NMRK limit, the complexity of the two-gluon CEV in this study is sufficient to support the suggestion made previously that a photon exchange mechanism may be responsible for certain observed discrepancies within hadron structure data. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings are experimentally verifiable through the synthesis of various colloidal particles grafted with polymers, enabling a direct comparison of predicted and observed behavior. Ultimately, this research will enable the design of materials with tailored properties by utilizing the unique properties of surface-tethered polymers. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We provide a method for calculating beta_1 for any graph by finding the largest independent set of the graph's neighborhood N_1, where the distance between points in this set is 2. We also develop an algorithm for calculating beta_k by converting the graph to a new version that takes into account distances of up to k between points and then identifying the largest independent set in this new version. This new algorithm allows us to calculate beta_3 for any graph efficiently, though doing so for graphs with more than 2 vertices in N_1* becomes NP-hard. We also discuss a method for identifying the smallest metric dimension of a graph by examining different independent sets in its truncated versions and we provide examples of graphs with a wide range of metric dimension values. Finally, we discuss some properties of beta_1 and beta_2 of a graph and how they relate to each other and to other graph properties. We also find a connection between the smallest metric dimension of a graph and the largest independent set in its N_1 and N_2 neighborhoods and we develop a method for calculating the truncated metric dimension of a graph by looking at its sub-graphs and we show that the standard metric dimension of a graph is equal to the truncated metric dimension of its version with distances up to k between points, where k is equal to the number of vertices in the graph's largest independent set. We also discuss some open questions about the properties of a graph's truncated metric dimension. We also discuss some applications of this property to GPS locationing and to finding a mobile device in a wireless network. We conclude by discussing the limitations of this property and some potential improvements to it. We also discuss some alternative versions of this property and we provide examples of graphs with a wide range of values of these properties. Finally, we discuss some open questions about these properties and we conclude by discussing some potential real-world applications of these properties. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. A key benefit is that this method allows for equal attention to be given to both bright and faint features in all-sky maps. For example, upon re-examining the all-sky maps from 2010 to 2019 with this method, researchers discovered the satellite had previously observed the giant radio loop GR 0430-619, first identified decades earlier. These findings suggest machine learning image enhancement can significantly expand our knowledge of the sky. Given its effectiveness, this approach may be a valuable tool for analyzing data from the Fermi satellite and other experiments, like the Chandra X-ray Observatory and XMM-Newton. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. This metric enables a fair comparison of the efficiency of action sequence-based solutions when dealing with various optimization problems. We further verify the effectiveness of our proposed solutions through comprehensive computational tests on diverse scenarios. We make available all computational test data and algorithm code. We explore the potential for action sequence-based solutions to tackle dynamic versions of static combinatorial optimization challenges by introducing a new framework and evaluating some of our obtained results. We provide a general framework for designing action sequence-based algorithms and an associated evaluation framework along with a demonstration of this design for the graph matching problem. We also examine an alternative general model and its application to the directed graph arborescence challenge, concluding that both models have merits and can yield optimal solutions in specific situations. We explore the differences between our basic model and other approaches such as simultaneous decision-making and provide a general model that encompasses both our model and the simultaneous decision-making model. We also provide a general algorithm for designing action sequence-based algorithms and evaluate some of our obtained results under this general model. We conclude by outlining some open challenges and possible research pathways in this domain. We provide a detailed description of all computational test data and algorithm code available for reference. 4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As our methods identified objects with 
abundant light from just one component of a binary, we compared their occurrence
rates to expectations based on the population of primary and secondary asteroids
as derived from existing studies. Our analysis revealed a significant discrepancy,

Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma. An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Moreover, this approach yields diverse, linguistically rich dialogue comparable to that found in genuine Dungeons and Dragons conversations. A notable outcome from our research is the creation of a publicly accessible dataset comprised of guided conversations derived from online streams of D&D games. This dataset, along with a code-used framework for a Dungeon Master training, is now made available for the research community. A notable finding from our research is also the outcome of human players preferrering the natural conversational style generated by a parallel attention-based approach over the more straightforward state-action-based method. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This research demonstrates the value of integrating topological principles with statistical methods to gain insights into the complex process of protein folding. Additionally, it highlights the potential of advanced topological models to uncover hidden dimensions in the structures of knotted proteins, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of their unique properties. By exploring the relationships between topology, geometry, and sequence in proteins with trefoil knots, this study paves the way for further investigation into the relationships between structure and function in all types of knotted proteins. A trefoil knot is the most common type of protein knot found in nature, found in approximately one out of every five proteins with knots. Understanding its intricate folding process will provide valuable insights into addressing the unfolding challenge of proteins with knots, a problem that has significant implications for the development of new protein therapies. Despite the significance of this issue, current protein therapies often fail due to the proteins' tendency to become knotted during transport from the laboratory to living organisms. Unraveling the mystery of protein knots will also enable the design of novel protein structures with enhanced stability, a critical component for creating effective enzyme-based biofuels and protein-based biomaterials. By exploring the intricate relationship between the sequence, geometry, and topology of proteins with trefoil knots, this study lays the groundwork for further investigation into protein structures with complex topological features. This knowledge will be essential for addressing the unfolding challenge of proteins with knots and creating novel enzyme-based biofuels and protein-based biomaterials. In addition to its scientific contributions, this research also demonstrates the potential of language models to facilitate breakthroughs in biologically complex challenges by providing a neural network-based interpretation of the study's findings. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, we establish that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of any blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is $ℤ_2\oplus ℤ_2$. Furthermore, we determine the area of these Lagrangian submanifolds through an application of a mirror correspondence, thereby gaining insight into their geometry. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields models that exhibit a 3% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, we find that this method proves cost-effective when compared to supervised counterfactual generation. Our method also enables seamless creation of diverse counterfactual data, thereby enabling the production of numerous high-quality instances per second. We have publicly disseminated the counterfactual datasets produced via this method, spanning over 300,000 instances in five diverse domains. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric called the Disentanglement Score that gauges a model's capacity to integrate its task knowledge in a disentangled manner. We leverage this metric to validate the effectiveness of our counterfactual data generation approach and show that it yields models with superior disentanglement properties. We have further integrated this method into a comprehensive learning framework that we call Inverted Learning and successfully applied it to obtain superior performance in three complex text-classification tasks with intricate causal structures. We have thoroughly evaluated the robustness of our method and the method's performance in the Inverted Learning setting on additional three classification tasks. Lastly, we explore a high-level extension to this method that we call Multi-World Learning and successfully apply it to a complex reasoning task that involves significant structural changes in the input data. We have thoroughly evaluated the methods' performance using a diverse range of baselines and variants of the learning approaches and found that the methods we present outperform the baselines in all evaluation metrics in every setting. We have further integrated the methods' code along with the datasets produced via the method into an open-source PyTorch code repository that we made publicly available. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This knowledge may contribute to the development of precise control over film/substrate relationships in complex materials systems. It's also shown that it's feasible to grow high quality Heusler films on graphene/sapphire substrates through a process that could potentially be scalable to industrial production methods. The material quality is assessed through a range of measurements including scanning tunneling microscopy, low energy electron diffraction, x-ray photon emission spectroscopy, resistivity, and magnetization. This research may also provide a pathway for creating remote epitaxially grown films of other materials. A additional finding in this study is the demonstration of a unique, highly efficient magnetic spin anti-aliasing effect, where the magnetic field is precisely half the expected value in order to switch the film's magnetic state. This effect is attributed to a unique, remote epitaxially induced structural property and may offer a breakthrough in the development of magnetic memory technologies that are energy efficient. A theoretical model of the remote epitaxial process is also presented, along with a description of the unique, epitaxially induced structural property that gives rise to this unique magnetic spin anti-aliasing effect. This model may be applicable to the understanding of remote epitaxy in other materials. A discussion on how this research may lead to the development of remote epitaxially grown films of other materials is also presented. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential secondary labels.  A novel multi-label sampling approach, called single positive multi-label sampling, is developed to generate additional training data based on this single label annotation.  To achieve this, a technique is established that first identifies all possible labels through a threshold-based approach, followed by a method to ensure diversity among generated labels by treating them as points in a high-dimensional space and applying a minimum distance requirement.  Experimental results show that this new approach enhances the generative model's performance on the dataset produced from single positive labels, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method and resulting in a significant reduction in the required annotations.  Furthermore, this method's effectiveness is validated across multiple datasets and conditions in the context of both low-resolution and high-resolution images.  The proposed technique is also adaptable to scenarios involving multiple conditions and limited data, to which a new approach is also introduced, extending the standard transference technique to the multi-condition, single positive setting, and demonstrating that our sampling method aligns with the standard definition of a conditional distribution. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. Notably, QASPER showcases the first instance of a Question Answering dataset centered around understanding documents, obtaining all data through controlled, supervised experiments, and featuring challenging information-seeking questions that do not ask for simple fact verification. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear. To address this challenge, our proposed approach develops a comprehensive framework for identifying and clarifying the meaning of acronyms in textual content, encompassing both user-contributed and web-scraped texts. This framework is an interactive web application that allows users to submit texts, identifies potential acronyms within that text, and accesses a vast thesaurus of definitions to provide possible clarifications for each identified acronym. If the provided definition is insufficient, the system enables user input to supplement the meaning. To further enhance the system's efficacy, we incorporate a mechanism for user feedback, enabling the improvement of its acronym-identification accuracy. The acronym-identification component leverages a combination of advanced techniques, including machine learning, substring patterns, and lexical resources, to pinpoint acronyms within the text. Conversely, to derive the acronym's definition, we employ a combination of natural language processing, including reverse engineering and definition extraction, aided by a vast repository of definitions available through the system. To facilitate seamless usage, the application is designed with a user-friendly interface and an engaging user experience in mind, all while boasting a robust and efficient architecture. Furthermore, we outline the outcomes obtained using this system on numerous benchmark datasets, showcasing its acronym-identification accuracy compared to other established approaches. The development of this system has also facilitated the creation of a comprehensive acronym-lookup dictionary, available for public perusal. The system's source code, user guidelines, and additional details are available for replication and further extension in our code repository. The acronym-identification component's complexity gives it a substantial footprint of approximately 220 million bytes. In contrast to other acronym-identification tools, this system excels in providing definitional clarifications. Nonetheless, the system exhibits limitations in acronym-identification accuracy, particularly in contexts replete with acronyms, due to its reliance on rule-based identification techniques. To overcome this constraint, we propose integrating machine learning models capable of acronym-identification, such as leveraging pre-trained models like BERT and transforming them into actionable Acronym-Entity-Relationship triples. The enhanced version of the system, MadDog2, employs a combination of rule-based and machine learning approaches, yielding notable gains in acronym-identification accuracy, especially in scenarios with multiple acronyms. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the case where the dark state condition is not met, either generally known as the abiotic case, or not at all, we derived an inelastic pendulum model with a diagonal spin potential. In the abiotic case, we derived an inelastic pendulum model with an anti-symmetric spin potential. Both models result in molecule-atom pair entanglements due to a virtual spin transfer from atoms to atoms and molecules to molecules. In the adiabatic case, we also derived an equation that relates the conversion rate from atoms to molecules and the effective three-body recombination rate. In the abiotic case, we found that the conversion rate from atoms to molecules is controlled by a collision that transfers spin in an "atom-molecule pendulum". The "atom-molecule pendulum" can also be used in large scale magnetic instability in condensates with multiple spin units. Additionally, the "atom-molecule pendulum" can be used in the creation of a diatomic BEC with a high degree of molecule-atom pair entanglements. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. In the case of experiments, this involves accessing the nodal lines through appropriate polarization and collecting data with sufficient momentum space resolution. Theoretically, it involves resolving the long-standing debate over the stability of topological nodal lines in momentum space. Additionally, this review outlines the potential for artificial materials to contribute substantially to the fundamental understanding of topological nodal lines. Finally, it highlights the potential for nodal lines to contribute to novel phenomena in optical phenomena, such as optical non-locality and oscillations, enabling both practical applications and a deeper understanding of topological nodal lines. Consequently, this review is of value to both Condensed Matter Physicists and Optical Scientists, as it provides an overview of the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and their realizations in optical systems. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our evaluation of a corresponding deep model, trained and tested on face images, reveals a substantial improvement in rematerialization and pose-induction tasks, demonstrating the importance of precise shadow rendering for robustness and accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/antitlo/efficient-shadows.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. We have developed a deep learning-based method that efficiently solves the shallow water equations with minimal external data, while also facilitating quick re-deployment to account for changes in riverbed topology. This new approach allows for rapid river flow velocity predictions without the need for detailed bathymetric data, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on the River Meuse in Netherlands. Furthermore, our algorithm is highly scalable and can be easily applied to the challenging problem of predicting flow velocities in coastal seas. We have open-sourced our code to promote the use of deep learning-based models in hydrodynamics and provide a demonstration of this approach using the deep learning framework TensorFlow. While our predictions are initially less accurate than traditional solutions, we show that substantial improvements can be achieved with relatively small datasets, leading to significantly faster computations. We have investigated various deep learning architectures and found that a simple multi-layer perceptron yields the best results in terms of prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. We have also explored the incorporation of external data, including satellite imagery and point measurements, to further enhance the performance of our predictor. We have obtained promising results and our method has potential applications in predicting flow velocities in oceans and atmospheres. We have released an open-source Python implementation of our method, which can be easily adapted to solve the Navier-Stokes equations. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the complex interactions between causal principles, statistical theory, and practical implementation issues. This paper addresses these challenges by providing a comprehensive overview of the state of the art, a detailed explanation of the underlying concepts, and a unified view of the field through a representation framework. We also outline an organizational structure for the field, identifying key research questions, and conclude with an exploration of potential future directions for development. We have appended this overview with a list of open-source code examples for reference purposes. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, EOWS shows comparable and even superior performance on standard classification tasks, showcasing its potential as a versatile and general-purpose deep learning loss function. The EOWS implementation is now available online. Its source code can be accessed at the specified repository URL. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. We invite the research community to engage with this innovative environment and contribute to its development, and we're excited to share the details of L2Explorer's design, implementation, and evaluation methods in further detail within this paper. We've also included a dedicated website highlighting the project, along with accompanying code available on GitHub under an permissive license to facilitate community involvement and collaboration. We've further outlined the scope and scope of the project, along with our vision for its future direction and potential research pathways in the accompanying overview provided in the appendix. We hope that L2Explorer will become a key platform for evaluating and comparing different lifelong learning approaches, and we look forward to contributing to the project's development and refinement in collaboration with our peers. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks by addressing these issues. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. To further reduce false positives, BNPS includes a spatial anti-aliasing technique that employs a proposal's center of mass to determine its class before sampling. Our approach demonstrates superior performance across multiple datasets for VRD tasks. Notably, SABRA achieves exceptional results on the VisStoke dataset, a recently introduced benchmark, and outperforms the current state-of-the-art baseline by a margin of 5%. Moreover, our results on the MVD and VisKinship datasets reveal a notable enhancement of up to 10% in accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhai-kai/SABRA. In conclusion, two acknowledged experts in the field have reviewed and approved the discovery presented here, recommending that further research be conducted to validate these findings, namely by analyzing recorded data from ground detectors in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Additionally, it is suggested that military owned satellite systems, such as DMSP and POES, hold valuable data that could contribute to a greater understanding of this phenomenon. 

In context to the presented data and supporting evidence, November 7th, 2004 is recognized as the second confirmed instance of solar neutron decay protons detected on Earth.

Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. Furthermore, this protocol was proven to be optimal. For UPBs in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 3$, it was shown that the number of unextendible states was the highest possible, given any of the three systems being in a qubit state, and this was linked to a previous result from Halder. Additionally, this finding was confirmed by a much simpler proof. For systems of four parties, it was proven that any UPB in $d_A \otimes d_B \otimes d_C \otimes d_D$ with more than $(d_A d_B)(d_C d_D)$ unextendible states has strong quantum nonlocality, establishing a minimum size requirement for this phenomenon in multipartite systems. This provides a more flexible and general condition than any previously known condition. In the case of four qubits, it was shown that the four-entanglement threshold for this phenomenon was located between the two previously known values. Lastly, this strong quantum nonlocality was demonstrated in some states with superposable effects, addressing a previous open question from Halder and others. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. The algorithm's simplicity and direct application to any survey design make it highly adaptable, and we provide evidence of this by applying it to CHAMAKO, a gasket-shaped survey with a large number of fibers. This algorithm will be an essential component of the SDSS-V, as its implementation could increase its target acquisition speed by up to five times. This paper is an extension of a previous study presented at the IAU 4th East Asian School of Astronomy in 2020.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from marmoset brain data. Notably, the models reproduced the abnormal theta rhythms commonly found in Parkinson's patients. This research may provide a groundwork for further exploration of disease mechanisms and development of novel treatments. In particular, we propose utilizing our model in the analysis of circuit-level alterations caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons. Additionally, we suggest investigating potential restoration pathways for the abnormal theta rhythms observed in Parkinson's disease. In the context of marmoset monkeys, maturational changes in brain structure and function will also be examined. This is the first Parkinson's disease model featuring a broad range of brain regions, from the cortex to the basal ganglia. A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial radii. The results show that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV cosmologies can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV cosmologies can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference based on cross-correlation. Additionally, the likelihood analysis confirms these distinctions and estimates the parameters as $f \sim -10^{-5}$ and $\sum m_\nu \sim 0.06$eV ($0.15$eV) for fR6 (fR5) cosmology. Furthermore, a mock observation from a fiducial fR6+$0.06$eV cosmology yields a $2.2\sigma$ preference for this specific cosmology when considering the four distinct cosmologies. Moreover, the integrated likelihood of $\sum m_\nu$ profiles also shows a $3.2\sigma$ difference between $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV cosmologies. The findings of this study highlight the significance of investigating the turn-around radii of cluster halos as a distinguishable feature to resolve the degeneracy between alternative gravity models and massive neutrinos. The research outcomes are valid for analyses of cluster halos at the present epoch from $N$-body simulations spanning a mass range from $10^{14}$ to $10^{15} M_\odot$. The methodology developed in this research provides a quantitative framework for differentiating between cosmologies by analyzing the probability distribution of turn-around radii to virial radii ratios. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. These outcomes facilitated a level of confidence in the readiness of the upgraded detector for further data collection. This project was conducted as part of an undergraduate research internship at CERN. Additionally, this study outlines the method used to activate and scan the eight pilot modules, each comprising eight sections, within the upgraded forward pixel detector. Although initially, there were issues with several modules, successful data collection was eventually achieved from all 64 sections. The analysis of data collected from these new components, the hit finding efficiency, and the track-hit residual patterns are also discussed in this study. These outcomes have given the upgrade team the confidence that the upgraded detector is ready for further data collection. This project was done as part of an undergraduate research internship at CERN. The reconstruction process used the CMS's established framework, converting raw data into base data objects and then mapping the particle path using the Global Tracker Algorithm. Following this, the hit efficiency and track-residual patterns were analyzed to validate the detector's performance. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. Due
to the constraints of character count in Twitter posts, traditional techniques for sentiment
analysis proved ineffective, and our proposed model successfully addressed these challenges.

This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. To build
a robust and scalable chat system, we also test the role-compliance of models
in our dataset by utilizing a newly developed evaluation toolkit that mimics real
human interactions over various roles and supports large-scale model assessments. 
Our research provides a data-driven framework that can be used to develop open-
domain dialogue systems with specific roles for various applications, such as
human-human dialogue simulation, virtual assistants, and chatbots that maintain
their personality and style across multiple conversations. Our code is available

data. Our evaluation toolkit is available at https://github.com/ghorpache/role-
evaluation-toolkit. Our work is further discussed in our paper that is available

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that, when taking risk into consideration, organic and minimally invasive management strategies significantly outperformed chemical-intensive approaches in 82% of cases. Furthermore, chemical-intensive management only ranked first in 8% of scenarios with consideration given to risk, whereas it never held the top position when results were based on yield and profit alone. This method offers a valuable solution for researching pesticide efficacy under uncertainty. The approach we presented can be adapted to research other complex farm management issues. Additionally, the results of our study provide valuable insights for strawberry growers and crop managers in Florida.
