This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Additionally, we find that in certain circumstances, the most energy-efficient method involves maintaining one part of the swimmer in a stationary position for extended periods, a phenomenon we verify by comparing our findings with established results obtained under a simplified model with no regenerative components. Furthermore, we find that in some cases, the fastest time to complete the cycle is not achieved at the optimal energy-efficient location. We also explore the impact of increasing size on our model, finding that it results in a modification of the underlying equation but one that still allows for optimal control solutions with limited switching points. We validate our analytical findings with numerical modeling and also visualize the phase plane for our model, identifying the locations of stable and unstable patterns for both small and large sizes. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting the potential applications of this research in replicating the optimal movements of marine animals that utilize flexible bodies to swim efficiently. We propose a method to optimize the physical parameters of these animals by applying periodic control to specific parts of their body and we outline a potential approach to achieve this level of control through external magnetic fields. We also explore the notion that life forms can evolve to control their movement efficiency by manipulating the switching points of their body's motion through natural selection, a concept we term 'phenotypic fluid control'. We provide a mathematical framework for this idea by defining a fitness function that is directly proportional to the cost of controlling the swimmer's movement, with the goal of minimizing this cost to maximize fitness. We then evolve this concept to a swimmer with multiple parts and we outline a pathway for a life form to evolve to utilize external resources to control its movement in complex environments through a process we term 'niche construction in fluid dynamics'. We also define two terms to describe different movement patterns in life forms, 'locomotion' to refer to movement through fluid environments and 'ambulation' to refer to movement through solid environments

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. To that end, this study introduces the concept of'structural mobility,' describing refrained urban exploration due to social distancing, which is shown to significantly contribute to decreased income diversity in urban settings. A better comprehension of the behavioral changes underlying these changes can aid policymakers in designing targeted urban mobility policies that promote diversity of urban encounters. A coarser analysis of visitation diversity in suburban settings reveals a less pronounced decline in diversity during the pandemic, with different underlying factors at play. A deeper examination of these settings may offer valuable insights into their specific social dynamics. A better understanding of the temporal changes in urban diversity during the pandemic is gained through the analysis of time-stamped visitation data, while the choice of mobility measures is justified through the inclusion of additional features in a classification experiment. A clear distinction is made between physical and social diversity in urban settings, along with the measures used to capture them, such as spatial and temporal entropy in addition to structural mobility. A clear methodology is provided for both our analysis and a range of related research studies. A separate section is dedicated to addressing potential methodological concerns about our analysis, along with a discussion of a key theoretical concept, the idea that diversity fosters a stronger more resilient community through various mechanisms. Finally, a range of potential pathways for future research in this area is outlined, along with a case study on visitation data in San Francisco during the pandemic. A broader implications section is also included, covering not just urban planning but also public health policy, management policy

Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Further examination into specific spectral features showed that the difference in hardness ratios might stem from additional X-ray emission components beyond the primary accretion stream. A possible explanation for this could be the impact of irregular accretion flows, which might be more prevalent in asynchronous polars due to their unique binary dynamics. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our reduction methods rely on the RBfoasim toolbox and our choices for the fine and reduced basis sizes will be determined experimentally. We'll also establish a metric to evaluate the effectiveness of our methods and our results will be visualized through isosurfaces of vorticity. Ultimately, our findings will be compared to the original, unfitted solution. We expect the higher complexity of the partitioned approach to lead to fewer degree of freedom reduction, which our results indeed confirm. Conversely, the monolithic approach yields similar accuracy with fewer degrees of freedom in the reduced model. This aligns with our expectations, as the partitioned approach involves solving more complex problems in each reduction iteration. We also observe a difference in the mesh transition region, attributing this to the approach used in constructing the coarse basis. This discrepancy vanishes when we employ a more sophisticated construction method, which our experiments validate. We plan to explore further methods for enhancing the RBM, such as utilizing more efficient solvers and developing more effective reduction techniques, as our results demonstrate the method's utility for computationally demanding FSI applications. Our implementation of the RBM is adaptable to various finite element methods, which we demonstrate by applying it to a contact problem using a conforming method. This capability will be particularly beneficial in applying the RBM to real-world, complex FSI scenarios, which often involve non-matching meshes in the fluid and solid domains. Our results also illustrate the RBM's potential for solving high-Reynolds-number flow scenarios, which typically pose significant challenges for other reduction methods. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Additionally, we apply DynaSOAr to solve a complex real-world application problem and present the DynaSOAr implementation, showing that it is both efficient and easy to use.  We also provide source code for all micro-benchmarks and applications presented in this paper, further showcasing its versatility and ease of adoption for object-oriented programming on SIMD devices.  Last but not least, we proffer a novel memory allocation approach called Alloc-Aot, a lock-free memory allocator that is also parallel, and successfully apply it to solve a distinct real-world application problem with superior memory management efficiency, resulting in a 5 times performance improvement and the ability to handle at least 2 times larger problems with the same memory.  Lastly, we explore the potential of our proposed DynaSOAr framework to facilitate the development of various high-performance computing applications on SIMD devices by allowing for the efficient allocation of memory for programs with inherent object structures. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks without upscaling, resulting in clearer boundary definitions. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations. The paper is dedicated to the memory of Dr. Maciek Wiesiak. 

The authors of this study have a further finding not mentioned in the abstract. This excess around neutrino directions was significant with a p-value of 0.0206 or 2.54σ, and had a characteristic scale of about 4 degrees. Additionally, if sources are broad enough (above 10 degrees) to encompass this excess, its significance would be below the 1σ threshold. This finding could provide a clue to understanding the origin of UHECRs and high-energy neutrinos if confirmed with more data. 

The paper reports the results from a comprehensive neutrino-UHECR correlation analysis that could be an important step in pinpointing the sources of these cosmic rays. Further research with upgraded and future neutrino and UHECR detection facilities such as the Accordion and the Pierre Auger Upgrade will be crucial in confirming these results and gaining a deeper insight into the origin of UHECRs and high-energy neutrinos.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements is ensured by the consistent relationship we found between stress and the angle of the rough surface in all three regimes. Our study also reveals the influence of surface roughness on the stick-slip behavior, identifying conditions that either prolong or shorten the duration of this phenomenon. Furthermore, we propose a model that explains the occurrence of the stationary soap film regime and calculates the stress experienced during slippage and stick-slip behavior. Additionally, we provide evidence that the stick-slip regime is a result of the interaction between surface defects and the film's symmetry. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems, ensuring minimal travel time, reduced congestion, and lower accident rates. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user adoption rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the optimal sensing strategy for this mobile sensing system, taking into consideration factors such as road segments to be covered, data collection timing, and the distribution of vehicles to maximize data reliability and reduce costs. Computational models, along with real-world data from over 20,000 vehicles in New York City, are utilized to evaluate and refine this approach, leading to significant cost reductions of up to 25% in expenses on gas, vehicle wear, and operator time for every dollar spent on data storage. The optimized scheme also results in an improvement of 10% in data reliability, reducing the likelihood of road conditions being incorrectly estimated by half. This study presents valuable insights that can be applied to other mobile sensing applications, surpassing existing challenges and opening up possibilities for the monitoring of urban infrastructure through real-time data collection. A significant aspect of this research is the introduction of innovative algorithms that can efficiently handle complex, dynamic scenarios, addressing current limitations in mobile sensing related to data processing. The development of a robust system for real-time data processing and analysis is also presented, capable of quickly interpreting the condition of urban roads and providing optimal solutions for routing vehicles to repair damaged sections priority-wise. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attributes such as biased language or sudden changes, and are able to produce more reliable scores by downweighting the influence of such samples. This approach outperformed existing methods and achieved comparable performance. As a result, we believe that the development of defense mechanisms such as this one is crucial for ensuring the reliability and validity of automated scoring systems. Furthermore, we recommend that the adoption of closed-source, commercial scoring platforms should be done with caution and that more research is needed to gain a deeper understanding of how these algorithms work. Finally, we propose that the creation of open-source, community-driven scoring platforms that operate on a transparent, accountable and fair principle would be highly beneficial. This approach would enable the development of more robust defense mechanisms and contribute to a greater understanding of the complex workings of these algorithms. This would also promote good practices that could be applied to other critical decision-making systems that rely heavily on the output of artificial intelligence algorithms. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. However, the challenge of successfully breaking down these complex variables into separate components for reward and state remains an area for further research. The developed theories and techniques are incorporated into a removal tool for the external state and reward variables, which is made available for public use. The code for this project can be found at the following repository https://github.com/cg1210/ER-Remover. The guidelines for utilizing the removal tool as a standalone library within other Python projects are provided in the README file of this repository. The distribution of the computation time for the reinforcement learning experiments is presented in multiple graphs, illustrating the significant acceleration achieved with the variable removal tool, particularly in environments involving complex external state and reward variables. The acceleration achieved with the variable removal tool is attributed to the substantial decrease in the dimensionality of the variables that can be controlled, as defined by the policy evaluation framework. The implications of this acceleration on the scalability of reinforcement learning experiments in complex environments are the focus of the conclusion. The conclusion is followed by a discussion on three potential applications of the variable removal tool: collaborative reinforcement learning learning, reinforcement learning learning with multiple agents, and the evaluation of multiple policies in a single environment. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A discussion on the implications of this exploration in relation to general Deep Learning is also included. We further establish a connection between GCNNs and the use of matching filters, suggesting this as a unified framework for all Deep Learning methodologies that can be built upon in further research. A connection between the spectral and spatial domains of data is also highlighted, along with a possible path for the optimization of GCNNs that is derived from this common framework. This exploration is applicable across all graph-structured data, regardless of the data source, providing a path for future research in the optimization of Deep Learning Algorithms. We also provide a possible solution to achieve this optimization, along with a proposed new Non-Destructive Sampling technique that can be applied to all Deep Learning Algorithms. This technique is then applied to a GCNN, resulting in a significant improvement in performance on multiple benchmark datasets. A comparison with current state-of-the-art techniques that leverage implicit differentiation shows that the new technique yields comparable performance with much less variance, as demonstrated across three distinct datasets. A possible extension of this research in the domain of implicit differentiation is also presented, along with a possible path for the optimization of Deep Learning Algorithms that is derived from this common framework. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics. This method allows us to deduce the operator spectrum for the Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we can utilize holomorphic duality to generalize our findings to theories of Yang-Mills with algebra sp(2N) and o(2N). This generalized case includes popular theories like N=4 Yang-Mills in four-dimensional space-time. The branes equivalent to the symmetries play a crucial role in predicting invariant objects within these theories, such as nilpotent operators in N=4 Yang-Mills. The structure of monopole operators in theories of Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) also follows the symmetries' fusion principles, as shown through the equivalent branes' combination rules. The fusion principles, branes, and combined monopole operators then result in the consistent combination of monopole operators in N=4 Yang-Mills, providing a holistic understanding of this theory. The rule that governs the combination of these monopole operators is determined by the fusion principles derived from the branes equivalent to the symmetries. This rule ensures that the combined monopole operators include both scalar and vector types, as well as an alternative, more complex type, encompassing both a nilpotent and a dual charge-carrying monopole operator for each given charge combination. The four distinct types of monopole operators are related to each other through their combination rules, which are dictated by the symmetries' fusion principles, as evidenced by the equivalent branes. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Notably, the VSSA-enabled technique yields accurate estimates even in deeply situated soft tissue with low compression, achieving precise measurements of lateral displacement in elastography. The study's findings provide a solid foundation for utilizing VSSA in ultrasound elastography applications. The VSSA framework's versatility allows its integration with other beamforming techniques and data analysis methods, making it a versatile solution for elastography. The study's significant contribution is the validation of VSSA's effectiveness in accurately estimating lateral tissue displacement under various compression conditions. The outcome shows that VSSA-facilitated accurate lateral displacement estimation enables the effective identification of tissue inhomogeneities in compression, a crucial requirement for the successful implementation of elastography in medical diagnostics. The research outcome is significant in the ultrasound imaging technology domain as it presents a breakthrough solution for accurately estimating lateral tissue displacement in ultrasound elastography. The study's findings are pertinent to the development of efficient algorithms for accurate displacement estimation in ultrasound elastography, a critical technology for the diagnosis and treatment of medical conditions such as breast cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders. The outcome of the study provides a solid foundation for the design of efficient elastography techniques that can detect and differentiate soft tissue abnormalities in compression, a critical requirement for the successful implementation of elastography in medical diagnostics. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This combination of forward reasoning and computability logic connections forms the basis for our proposal of a logical pseudocodes language, which we demonstrate through implementation with the example of solving the 2D maze problem. This example is also used to illustrate a derived property preservation theorem, which guarantees that the safe states in the solution algorithm correspond to success in the original maze solving task. This achievement is significant because it reveals the potential of our proposed method for deriving secure algorithms from specifications that ensure preservation of specific properties. This idea is further explored in our discussion of a hypothetical property-preserving compiler in the context of our framework. A significant insight derived from our exploration of logical pseudocodes may also be an advancement in the field of programming languages, where the relationship between algorithms and proofs is shown to provide a more fundamental and unified view of types, in effect making the concept of types superfluous. This realization leads to a proposal for a new type system based solely on the preservation of specific properties, which we believe is both more flexible and easier to grasp than traditional type systems. This idea is put forward as a potential solution to the issue of type systems causing complexity in programming, which could potentially be resolved by a type system that the authors propose calling the "Simple Type System" (STS). This STS is then put forward as a candidate for a fundamental type system that could serve as a unifying force across various type systems. This proposal is subject to critique through the example of a maze solver program, which shows how easily a derivation based on safe states can fail when trying to apply the STS in reverse. This reverse application of the STS is attempted as a demonstration of a property-preserving compiler, which ultimately results in a discussion on the role of the cut rule in the conversion of logical pseudocodes to actual code. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset will be entirely colored with a specific color in a Boolean lattice. Recent work has led to the determination of Boolean Ramsey numbers for specific instances, and this paper aims to build on that by investigating the same concept for V-shaped posets and identifying minimum posets containing the Ramsey property in Boolean lattices of a particular size. Another area of research within this paper focuses on Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers which involve identifying either a monochromatic structure or a structure with different color components within a Boolean lattice. This study explores this concept for V-shaped posets and their antichains. A significant achievement of this research is the identification of Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers for particular instances of V-shaped posets, and some limits on these numbers. Furthermore, this paper introduces the concept of Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers for sets of posets and investigates this property for V-shaped posets and their antichains in Boolean lattices of a particular size. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset or its antichain will be entirely colored with different color components in a Boolean lattice. Finally, this paper concludes with some open problems and potential directions for further research in this area. A significant achievement of this research is the identification of Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers for specific instances of V-shaped posets, and some limits on these numbers, and this could provide a foundation for exploring the same concept for other types of posets. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. We also theoretically validate the optimality of our approach within a specific context. This hierarchical framework has the potential to generalize to larger environments beyond grid worlds. We accompany our algorithmic innovation with a code release, accessible via https://github.com/AAE2020/HPEGE. Via empirical analysis and visualizations, we gain further insight into the behavior of stochastic players in our hierarchical setting. Finally, we reinterpret our hierarchy as a multi-agent collaboration scenario, consisting of multiple evasive entities working together to maximize their collective chances of evading the pursuer. This led us to develop an alternative approach, Hierarchical Coordinated Policy Iteration (HCPI), which employs a coordinated iteration scheme to optimize the performance of the entire group. This new approach, though not directly linked to our primary result, shows computational efficiency benefits and could serve as a foundation for broader applications involving the coordination of multiple agents. Overall, our research provides a pioneering attempt to divide complex multi-agent games into hierarchical components, while our results, although derived within the context of pursuit-evasion games, could potentially serve as a foundation for more general applications involving the coordination of multiple agents. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. We explore how the 'cyclic' condition is satisfied by examining the associated order statistics and probability cumulatives, and discuss the implications of our findings in the context of decision-making under uncertainty. Last, we consider a related 'weak' definition of a 'cyclic' probability and associated 'nontransitive' probability and our results hold for this definition as well.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images during training. The proposed architecture leverages this adaptive capability to consolidate the training of both directions with a single generator, doing so while minimizing memory requirements and processing speeds. In our experiments, the results show this method outperforms the conventional cycleGAN method using two generators and also delivers superior performance compared to non-deep learning denoising methods. Moreover, our model exhibits compactness, with a significant reduction in model size compared to the two-generator cycleGAN model. We were able to achieve comparable performance with only approximately half the number of parameters. Our method has the added benefit of being straightforward to implement and there is no model escalation during training, which is a major advantage over other deep learning methods. Our code has been made publicly available on the MIMIC-CT dataset, with a demo video available online. Our research suggests this efficient, unsupervised low-dose CT denoising method has immense potential for use in clinical practice, particularly in situations where storage and computation resources are limited. As a result, this method could provide a viable solution for upgrading the quality of CT images in clinical settings without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. Overall, this method delivers superior performance when compared to non-deep learning denoising methods and achieves comparable performance to two-generator cycleGAN models but with only half the number of parameters. Furthermore, our method has the added benefit of being straightforward to implement and there is no model escalation during training, which is a major advantage over other deep learning methods. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes. Moreover, ALM-ConvAI researchers find SPACE-2's representations exhibit superior performance on downstream tasks across three text-to-text task-oriented dialog understanding benchmarks in the TAOGLUE benchmark. This finding is further verified by verifications tests. Additionally, SPACE-2's embeddings' diversity and distinctiveness are validated through multiple evaluation metrics across three text-to-text task-ooriented dialog understanding datasets in the DiverseDialogEval benchmark. The evaluation evidence suggests that SPACE-2's unmatched performance can be attributed to its ability to capture diversity and distinctiveness in dialog understanding tasks. Consequently, this method serves as a premier starting point for participating researchers in the DialoGLUE and TAOGLUE challenges. To put its outstanding performance into perspective, this study's model ranks number one in almost every task across both dialog understanding and tao challenges leaving a considerable margin between itself and second placed model. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments compared three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved modifying evaluation conditions and reassessing the methods under these new standards. These experiments led to a conclusion that high scores derived from the methods, especially the direct prediction approach, may be inflated by biases present in the evaluation toolkit rather than an indication of the methods' effectiveness. As such, more robust evaluation procedures are needed to accurately assess these methods and potential alternatives. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements, the focus isn't solely on recovering the most likely image, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a diverse range of images from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which we tested on deblurring and MRI applications. Our approach outperformed current methods with ease. We also demonstrated that our method generates a diverse range of images from the posterior distribution, achieving this through the use of optimal transport theory. We're the first to show that boosting the GAN's discriminator improves its generator output, achieving this by structuring our training process in a way that mimics the inverse problem we're trying to solve. We're also the first to use the initial measurement data to train our GAN, which we integrated into a Bayesian framework. We validated our approach through synthetic and real-world MRI data tests. We're currently exploring ways to apply our approach to more complex imaging problems, such as MRI enhancement using multiple measurements types. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz (THz) bandwidths. However, THz communications have very limited coverage and are confined to short-distance connections, constraining applications to single-hop or multi-hop wireless networks. We are investigating single-hop connections, focusing on optimized beam training under the influence of fast-throttling phase noises and angular distortions, critical factors in THz communications. To mitigate these impacts, we are developing a novel rapid beam training method utilizing reinforcement learning, capable of adapting to changing channel conditions without requiring channel state information. Simulations show our proposed scheme provides up to 350% improvement in energy efficiency and a 50% reduction in time delay compared to existing methods. By optimizing beam selection, we are also achieving a 50% increase in data transfer rate in the presence of phase noise and distortions, an otherwise significant limitation in THz communications. We verify the efficacy of our scheme both analytically and through simulation. Additionally, we apply our beam training technique to a multi-user THz communication system, presenting a 4G THz testbed to demonstrate the feasibility of our approach. We also explore the potential of our scheme to be extended to 5G and 6G wireless communications systems. We complement our theoretical discussion with an overview of relevant work, an in-depth analysis of the proposed scheme, and a review of the implemented numerical results but conclude by highlighting several open research issues and potential solutions. We also offer a framework for evaluating the performance of beam training schemes in the context of fast-throttling phase noises and angular distortions that affect THz communications. We utilize this framework to assess the efficacy of our proposed method, even considering the impacts of phase noise and distortions in THz communications. We validate our analytical findings with extensive numerical results obtained using a customized version of MATLAB, releasing the simulation code as an open resource for researchers to replicate our results and explore the performance of our scheme in different scenarios. We anticipate our proposed rapid beam training method will contribute to the successful development of next-generation wireless devices that can maximize data transfer rates in THz communications systems. We also explore the potential of our scheme to be extended to 5G and 6G wireless communications systems. We also offer a framework for evaluating the performance of beam training schemes

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This particular screen is thought to be responsible for scintillating pulsar signals towards the Earth and may affect other radio signals passing through this region. Additionally, the velocity of this screen was found to be 10.5 km/s, aligned with the direction towards the center of the Sun, and its minor axis was determined to be 0.32 AU. This research demonstrates the capability of pulsar scintillation observations to reveal and study the interstellar medium in the line of sight to these distant celestial objects. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of selecting pulsars that transmit clear and undistorted radio signals, such as PSR B1133+16, for a deeper understanding of the physics governing the transmission and reception of radio waves through the interstellar medium. In the process, it identifies a hidden structure in the local environment surrounding the pulsar, specifically within the Local Bubble, and provides a new method for detecting voids in the interstellar medium. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Notably, QPNet achieves comparable speech quality to state-of-the-art network architectures but with significantly fewer parameters. This flexibility in parameter usage makes QPNet an attractive model for generative raw waveform applications with limited data. Furthermore, pre-trained QPNet features serve as a viable alternative to MFCCs for speech classification tasks, offering advantages in efficiency and scalability. The model's code and data are publicly available for use and adaptation. Nonetheless, some aspects of the proposed architecture rely on bespoke components and, thus, can likely be further improved through additional research in autoregressive generative models, convolutional neural networks, and signal processing. In particular, the fixed auxiliary feature learning approach for dynamic network architecture changes can probably be enhanced with advancements in neural network dynamics and multiple-feature learning strategies. Similarly, the cascaded network design for signal processing is primarily tailored to speech and other specific quasi-periodic signal types and probably can be further improved through the application of more general signal processing techniques. In the context of WN and its derivatives, the proposed innovations almost certainly can be used to create high-fidelity audio generation models with superior pitch control properties. This is especially evident in the evaluation results showing that QPNet delivers significantly better quality audio than the baseline WN model, particularly in speech and music audio files. Additionally, the model's quality is consistently better when used to synthesize audio files from a wider frequency range than the training data. This is a key advantage over other state-of-the-art network architectures, such as Transformer-based and multi-band speech synthesis models, which either have more parameters or are not as flexible in terms of frequency

The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. Swapping the normal lead for a high-resistance lead introduces additional signatures that can aid in differentiating a Majorana peak; specifically, the signature for a Majorana mode involves a cross over in conductance as temperature decreases, displaying a greater value when comparing left-to-right versus right-to-left measurement approaches. This phenomenon occurs due to the interplay between tunneling a high-resistance lead and temperature within the bulk material. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. An optimized mesh design is shown to yield superior results, compared to alternative methods such as the traditional Nitsche interface treatment. Further development and potential extensions for this approach are also discussed, including potential extensions beyond acoustic scattering, such as elastic scattering, as well as potential connections with other related methods. Computational results for both 2D and 3D scenarios are presented, demonstrating the method's efficacy in solving real-world problems, including the scattering of elastic waves, as well as time-domain wave propagation in 3D. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. However, further research is needed to fully validate these conclusions due to the limited size and nature of the pyroxene mineral samples available for analysis. Nonetheless, this study provides valuable new insights into the water content and D isotope signatures within the inner Solar System, shedding light on the water delivery to Mars. It suggests that Mars should have had more water with higher D-poor isotopic signatures than previously accounted for, likely as a result of being 2-3 million kilometers closer to the Sun than Earth during planetary accretion. This enhanced water delivery to Mars could have significantly altered its surface, possibly preventing the development of a stable atmosphere and thereby further consolidating its status as the planet with the most pronounced water deficiency in the Solar System.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Our open-source code also facilitates zero-shot machine translation application to speech-to-text. With zero-shot translation for additional language pairs proven feasible, our models hold considerable potential for multilingual speech-to-text. We explore this capability through the generation of synthetic data but identify room for further research in this domain. Our model's ability to learn multiple speech recognition tasks also serves as a single-system alternative to conventional two-stage approaches, reducing the amplification of inaccuracies associated with these methods. Our models demonstrate superior performance to multistage baselines in English speech recognition and outperform single-stage baselines in Latin speech recognition. Our research lays the groundwork for further exploration of zero-shot learning in speech-to-text. We explore the domain overlap with zero-shot machine translation but identify distinct difficulties, including greater text-audio disparities. Our research into relational machine learning, which learns multiple related tasks, reveals that zero-shot speech-to-text stands out as the most complicated task. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold valuable implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. Additionally, we identify that in many cases the total magnetic moment falls short of anticipating due to a discrepancy in the variation of orbital occupation with electron-electron coupling and spin-orbit coupling across the 4d and 5d periods. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it highlights an interesting result regarding the monodromy of the relative I-functions in the context of genus zero. Lastly, it outlines an interesting direction for future research regarding the extension of these results to a broader class of toric complete intersections. This research was presented at the 2021 virtual conference of the Canadian Mathematical Society.

Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be solved accurately, even with a grid cell size as small as $10^{-12}$. In our experiments, we compare our method with a standard FFT-based approach for simple domains and then apply it to solving volume integral equations using a boundary integral method. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves comparable performance to FFT-based methods for smooth domains, while also showing significant improvement in solving boundary value problems and volume integral equations on complex grids. In particular, solving a volume integral equation on a grid of $16\times 16$ cells is $4.5$ times faster than the FFT-based method. Our method also enables solving problems on much finer grids, with improvements of up to $10^4$ times in solving boundary value problems. In addition, our method allows solving problems with non-smooth boundaries, providing a significant breakthrough in computational science and potentially leading to new applications in physics and engineering. Furthermore, this method can be adapted to calculate harmonic differences and dipoles efficiently. Our code is publicly available for download.
